stem: A 26-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department 1 hour after having a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure. He has never had a seizure previously or any episode of jerking, staring, confusion, or memory loss. He has had no recent illness and has no history of neurological problems. Birth and development were normal. There is no family history of seizures or epilepsy. He takes no medication and does not use illicit drugs. His vital signs are normal. Neurological findings are unremarkable. Results of laboratory studies show a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
why_right: This is a first-time generalized tonic-clonic seizure in an adult with no provoking cause: normal CBC and metabolic panel, no drugs, no illness. After history and labs exclude provoked causes, the next step is neuroimaging to exclude a structural lesion, and in the Emergency Department a head CT is the fastest initial study. EEG follows to classify the seizure and estimate recurrence risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. ECG: right when the event may be syncope or arrhythmia (e.g. collapse with brief jerks, exertional or cardiac history); this is a clear generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
B. EEG: part of every first seizure workup, but it comes after imaging; it classifies the seizure and predicts recurrence rather than excluding an urgent structural cause.
D. Lumbar puncture: right when fever, meningism or immunosuppression suggest CNS infection, or SAH is suspected with a normal CT; none here, and imaging should precede LP.
key_concept:
First unprovoked seizure workup order.
  • 1. History: confirm seizure, exclude mimics (syncope)
  • 2. Exclude provoked causes: glucose, electrolytes, drugs, alcohol
  • 3. Neuroimaging: CT in the ED, MRI is the more sensitive elective study
  • 4. EEG
  • Epilepsy = 2 unprovoked seizures more than 24 h apart, or 1 with high recurrence risk (EEG or MRI abnormality)
exam_pearl: Normal labs after a first adult seizure push you to imaging; fever or meningism would push you to LP.

stem: A 60-year-old man is found to have elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup. He has no symptoms, and physical examination is unremarkable. ECG, CBC, electrolytes, renal function tests, and urine analysis are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next option in management?
OptD: Repeat office blood pressure measurement in 3 months
highlight_terms_source: elevated blood pressure during a routine checkup
why_right: An elevated reading at a "routine checkup" in an asymptomatic man with a normal examination, ECG, renal function and urinalysis (no end organ damage) does not yet establish hypertension. The next step is to confirm the diagnosis with out of office monitoring, ambulatory (ABPM) or home BP, which also excludes white coat hypertension.
why_wrong_block:
A. Echocardiography is not needed before diagnosis is confirmed; it is for suspected LVH, murmurs or heart failure.
B. Starting drugs on a single reading risks treating white coat hypertension; immediate treatment is reserved for very high BP or end organ damage.
D. Waiting 3 months for another office reading delays diagnosis and does not exclude white coat effect; ABPM or HBPM is the recommended confirmation.
key_concept:
Raised clinic BP: confirm with ABPM (or HBPM) before labelling or treating.
  • No end organ damage + one high reading: ABPM/HBPM
  • Very high BP or end organ damage (retinopathy, AKI, papilledema): treat or refer urgently without waiting
  • Baseline workup: ECG, urea and electrolytes, urine dip, lipids, glucose, fundoscopy
  • ABPM excludes white coat hypertension
exam_pearl: Normal workup + one high reading = confirm first; end organ damage = act now.

stem: A 65-year-old man was brought to the Emergency Room by his wife after she noticed he was confused and behaving in a strange way. He had no fever, cough, shortness of breath, chest pain, headache, abdominal pain, vomiting, or loss of consciousness. He is known to have type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and osteoarthritis, and is on insulin, metformin, candesartan, hydrochlorothiazide, aspirin, and atorvastatin. Examination reveals that he is conscious but disoriented. Left leg power is 2/5, while the other limbs are 5/5. There is decreased sensation in the left leg. Other neurological exams are normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his symptoms and signs?
highlight_terms_source: confused and behaving in a strange way
decreased sensation in the left leg
why_right: A 65-year-old with vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia) has left leg weakness 2/5 with left leg sensory loss while the other limbs are normal. The leg area of the motor and sensory cortex lies on the medial hemisphere, supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, so this is a right ACA stroke. Frontal lobe involvement explains the confusion and strange behavior.
why_wrong_block:
A. Migraine: there is no headache, and a fixed focal deficit in an older patient with vascular risk factors is stroke until proven otherwise.
B. Right MCA stroke: causes contralateral face and arm weakness greater than leg (with neglect in non-dominant lesions); here the arm is 5/5 and only the leg is affected.
D. Basilar artery stroke: gives brainstem and cerebellar signs (cranial nerve palsies, vertigo, ataxia, crossed or bilateral deficits, reduced consciousness), not an isolated unilateral leg deficit.
key_concept:
Localize stroke by which body part is worse:
  • ACA: contralateral leg > arm, behavior change, abulia, urinary incontinence
  • MCA: contralateral face and arm > leg, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant)
  • PCA: contralateral homonymous hemianopia
  • Lacunar: pure motor face = arm = leg, no cortical signs
  • Basilar/vertebral: crossed signs, cranial nerves, ataxia, coma
exam_pearl: Leg worse than arm = ACA; face and arm worse than leg = MCA.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with recurrent seizures and cognitive dysfunction. She is subsequently diagnosed with glioblastoma multiforme (see lab results). Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatremia?
why_right: Glioblastoma multiforme is a CNS lesion, and CNS disease (tumor, trauma, infection, stroke, hemorrhage) is a major cause of SIADH through hypothalamic dysfunction or inappropriate ADH release. Excess ADH causes water retention and euvolemic hyponatremia with concentrated urine, which can itself worsen seizures and cognition.
why_wrong_block:
A. Salt-wasting nephropathy is right with renal tubular disease causing hypovolemic hyponatremia with high urinary sodium; nothing here suggests renal disease or volume depletion.
B. Primary polydipsia is right in psychiatric patients drinking large volumes, with maximally dilute urine; here a brain tumor gives a direct SIADH mechanism.
C. Low-solute intake (beer potomania, tea and toast diet) can cause hyponatremia, but soft drinks are not a recognized cause in this setting.
key_concept:
SIADH: euvolemic hyponatremia, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine.
  • CNS causes: tumors, trauma, meningitis, stroke, SAH
  • Lung causes: small cell carcinoma, pneumonia
  • Drugs: carbamazepine, SSRIs, cyclophosphamide
  • Urine sodium high with normal renal, thyroid and adrenal function
  • Treat: fluid restriction; hypertonic saline only if severe symptoms
exam_pearl: Brain lesion + hyponatremia = SIADH; if the patient is volume depleted after neurosurgery or SAH, think cerebral salt wasting instead.

stem: A 26-year-old man with type I diabetes mellitus on insulin presents to the clinic for regular follow-up. He is asymptomatic (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment? BP:150/90
why_right: A young type 1 diabetic with BP 150/90 (and, on the lab sheet of this recall, proteinuria) has early diabetic nephropathy. An ACE inhibitor lowers BP and is nephroprotective: it reduces intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, slowing progression. ACE inhibitor or ARB is first-line in diabetics at any age.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diuretics lower BP but have no antiproteinuric effect; a thiazide-like diuretic is an add-on (step 2) rather than first choice in a diabetic.
B. Calcium channel blockers lack the kidney-protective effect; they are first-line in non-diabetics over 55 or of African or Caribbean origin, or as an add-on.
C. Beta-blockers do not protect the kidney and can mask hypoglycemia in an insulin-treated patient; they are used for specific indications such as post-MI or rate control.
key_concept:
Diabetes + hypertension or albuminuria = ACE inhibitor (or ARB).
  • Mechanism: efferent arteriolar dilation, lower glomerular pressure
  • Give even when normotensive if albuminuria is present
  • Side effects: cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia
  • Avoid in pregnancy
  • Step 2: add CCB or thiazide-like diuretic
exam_pearl: "Diabetic" + "most appropriate antihypertensive" = ACE inhibitor unless pregnant (then labetalol or nifedipine).

stem: A 34-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of jaundice and upper abdominal discomfort. She is a known case of SLE on hydroxychloroquine. She also gave a history of pruritus and fatigue. Clinical examination revealed obesity and hepatomegaly. US Abdomen: Showed enlarged liver with bright coarse echogenicity. Viral Hepatitis: Negative. ANA: 1:640 (High). Liver Biopsy: Interphase hepatitis with plasma cells. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Young woman with another autoimmune disease (SLE), very high transaminases, ANA 1:640, raised globulin and a biopsy showing interface hepatitis with plasma cells: this is autoimmune hepatitis. First-line treatment is corticosteroids (prednisolone), with or without azathioprine as a steroid-sparing agent.
why_wrong_block:
B. Methotrexate is not a standard treatment for autoimmune hepatitis and is itself hepatotoxic; it is used for rheumatoid arthritis or as an SLE add-on.
C. Vitamin E with weight loss treats NASH; the obesity and bright liver are distractors, because the biopsy shows plasma cell interface hepatitis, not steatohepatitis.
D. Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line for primary biliary cholangitis (cholestatic pattern with high ALP, AMA positive); here the pattern is hepatocellular with only mildly raised ALP.
key_concept:
Interface hepatitis with plasma cells = autoimmune hepatitis = prednisolone ± azathioprine.
  • AIH type 1: ANA, anti-smooth muscle antibody
  • AIH type 2: anti-LKM1, anti-liver cytosol
  • High IgG/globulin supports AIH
  • PBC: AMA, high ALP, pruritus, treat with ursodeoxycholic acid
  • PSC: p-ANCA, ulcerative colitis, MRCP beading
  • NASH: obesity, steatohepatitis on biopsy, weight loss ± vitamin E
exam_pearl: Pruritus and obesity tempt you toward PBC or NASH; the biopsy (plasma cells, interface hepatitis) decides.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed version highlights A; restated version on next page (with lab table: direct bilirubin 32, total bilirubin 43, AST 654, ALT 734, ALP 129, GGT 60, globulin 43) gives Answer: A (MG).

stem: Which of the following is the best oxygen delivery system in a patient with Pulmonary Disease?
why_right: In chronic lung disease such as COPD, high uncontrolled oxygen can worsen CO2 retention (V/Q mismatch, Haldane effect and loss of hypoxic drive), so oxygen must be controlled. A Venturi mask delivers a fixed, precise FiO2 regardless of breathing pattern, allowing titration to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92% without worsening hypercapnia.
why_wrong_block:
A. A simple face mask gives a variable, imprecise FiO2 and needs high flow to avoid CO2 rebreathing; it suits short-term moderate oxygen needs in patients not at risk of CO2 retention.
B. A rebreathing or reservoir bag delivers high, uncontrolled oxygen, risking CO2 narcosis in COPD; it is for critically hypoxic patients without CO2 retention, such as trauma or shock.
C. A nasal cannula is acceptable at low flow, but its FiO2 varies with the patient's breathing, so it is not the most precise; it suits stable patients and long-term home oxygen.
key_concept:
COPD oxygen = controlled oxygen via Venturi mask, target SpO2 88 to 92%.
  • Venturi: fixed precise FiO2 (low concentrations)
  • Nasal cannula: low flow, variable FiO2
  • Simple mask: moderate, variable FiO2
  • Non-rebreather reservoir: high FiO2, uncontrolled
  • Drowsy COPD on high oxygen = CO2 retention: reduce oxygen, check ABG
exam_pearl: "Best" delivery in COPD means most precise, not most oxygen: Venturi.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option D also marked with **.

stem: An elderly patient with end-stage metastatic cancer (I don't remember the type of the cancer) She is in palliative care and started to get aggressive and confused, and the staff couldn't calm her down. What's the best drug to give her?
why_right: An elderly palliative patient who becomes acutely confused and aggressive has hyperactive delirium. After looking for reversible causes, the drug of choice when non-drug measures fail is a low-dose antipsychotic, typically haloperidol, which calms agitation without worsening confusion.
why_wrong_block: B. Lorazepam and other benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and cause paradoxical agitation and sedation in the elderly; they are first-line only for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium or seizures, and are added in refractory terminal agitation.
key_concept:
Agitated delirium (including palliative care): treat the cause, non-drug measures, then haloperidol.
  • Look for reversible causes: infection, drugs (opioids), hypercalcemia, retention, hypoxia
  • Haloperidol: low dose, oral or subcutaneous
  • Benzodiazepines: alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, seizures
  • Benzodiazepine as add-on in refractory terminal agitation
  • Avoid antipsychotics in Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia
exam_pearl: Delirium + agitation = haloperidol; the exception that flips it to a benzodiazepine is alcohol withdrawal (or Parkinson/Lewy body disease, where haloperidol is avoided).

stem: A 39-year-old man diagnosed with pancreatic cancer develops a swollen left lower limb during hospitalization. Examination reveals a tender, erythematous swelling affecting the left leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: swollen left lower limb during hospitalization
why_right: He has two strong VTE risk factors: pancreatic cancer (one of the most thrombogenic malignancies) and hospitalization (immobility). A new unilateral, tender, erythematous, swollen left leg in this setting is DVT until proven otherwise, and should be confirmed with compression Doppler ultrasound.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lymphedema is chronic, painless, slowly progressive swelling (after nodal surgery or radiotherapy), not an acute tender red leg.
B. Cellulitis can mimic DVT but is right when there is fever, a skin breach or wound and spreading, well-demarcated warmth; here there is no entry point and two major VTE risk factors.
C. A ruptured Baker cyst is right with sudden calf pain in a patient with knee arthritis or a known popliteal cyst; there is no knee history here.
key_concept:
Unilateral painful swollen leg + VTE risk factor = DVT; confirm with duplex ultrasound.
  • Risk factors: malignancy, immobility/hospitalization, surgery, pregnancy, OCP, prior VTE
  • Pancreatic cancer: highly thrombogenic (migratory thrombophlebitis, Trousseau)
  • Mimics: cellulitis, ruptured Baker cyst, lymphedema, muscle injury
exam_pearl: Erythema does not mean cellulitis: without fever or a skin breach, a red swollen leg in a cancer inpatient is DVT.

stem: pt long standing DM came with 2 day history of WBC 18 with cellulitis tx:
why_right: A diabetic with cellulitis and a raised WBC (18) needs systemic antibiotics that reliably cover the usual culprits, Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus. Clindamycin covers both streptococci and staphylococci (including many community MRSA strains) and penetrates skin and soft tissue well, so it is the keyed empiric choice among these options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ciprofloxacin: weak against streptococci, so it is a poor choice for simple cellulitis; it is chosen for Gram negative infections such as pyelonephritis or Pseudomonas.
C. Vancomycin: reserved for severe or septic cellulitis, known MRSA, or failure of first line therapy; a 2 day cellulitis without shock does not need it first.
D. Meropenem: a broad spectrum carbapenem for febrile neutropenia or severe polymicrobial/resistant Gram negative sepsis; overkill for uncomplicated cellulitis.
key_concept:
Cellulitis = streptococci + S. aureus: pick an agent that covers Gram positives.
  • Mild: oral anti staphylococcal penicillin/cephalexin, or clindamycin (also if penicillin allergic)
  • Systemic features: IV therapy
  • Severe/septic or MRSA: vancomycin
  • Necrotizing infection signs: urgent surgery + broad cover
  • Febrile neutropenia: antipseudomonal beta lactam (e.g. meropenem)
exam_pearl: Quinolones (ciprofloxacin) miss streptococci, so they are the classic wrong answer for cellulitis; vancomycin only if severe or MRSA.

stem: Case of HBV Hx of blood transfusion 10 years ago HBs Ag +ve IgG +ve HBe Ag +ve ::
key_concept:
HBV serology decoder.
  • HBsAg +: current infection; persisting >6 months = chronic
  • Anti-HBc IgM +: acute; IgG + with HBsAg +: chronic
  • HBeAg +: active replication, high infectivity
  • Anti-HBe + / HBeAg negative: low replication (inactive carrier if ALT normal, DNA low)
  • Anti-HBs + with anti-HBc IgG +: recovered
  • Anti-HBs + alone: vaccinated
exam_pearl: IgM vs IgG anti-HBc decides acute vs chronic; HBeAg decides active vs inactive.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 35-year-old Indian man presents to the Emergency Department with lethargy, weight loss, and headache for 3 months. He has a history of contact with a tuberculosis patient several years ago. His neurological and ophthalmologic examination are unremarkable. He has a positive polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
OptB: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and diuretics
OptC: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and acyclovir
OptD: Isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol and dexamethasone
why_right: A man from an endemic area with 3 months of lethargy, weight loss and headache, a TB contact history and a positive M. tuberculosis PCR (the referenced labs, presumably CSF) has tuberculous meningitis. TB meningitis is treated with the four-drug regimen plus adjunctive dexamethasone, which reduces mortality by limiting inflammation, vasculitis and complications.
why_wrong_block:
A. The four-drug regimen alone is right for pulmonary TB, but in TB meningitis it is incomplete without corticosteroids.
B. Diuretics are not part of standard TB meningitis treatment; hydrocephalus is a complication handled separately (drainage or shunt when obstructive), not a reason to add diuretics routinely.
C. Acyclovir is for HSV or VZV encephalitis and is added empirically only while the cause is unknown; the PCR here confirms tuberculosis.
key_concept:
Meningitis treatment by cause
  • TB meningitis = RIPE + dexamethasone
  • Bacterial = ceftriaxone + vancomycin + dexamethasone
  • HSV/VZV encephalitis = acyclovir
  • Unknown cause empirically = ceftriaxone + vancomycin + acyclovir (+ dexamethasone)
  • Pulmonary TB = RIPE alone
exam_pearl: TB meningitis is the classic setting where dexamethasone is added to anti-TB drugs; uncomplicated pulmonary TB is the four drugs alone.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: D (option D also highlighted).

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Emergency Room with productive cough, fever, and dyspnea for 3 days. Chest examination reveals evidence of consolidation at the right lower lung field. Baseline laboratory studies, two blood cultures, and sputum samples for cultures and gram stain are obtained. Which of the following is the most appropriate empiric antimicrobial regimen?
highlight_terms_source: productive cough, fever, and dyspnea for 3 days
consolidation at the right lower lung field
why_right: Productive cough, fever and dyspnea for 3 days with right lower lobe consolidation in a community patient is community acquired pneumonia. He is being worked up in the ER with blood and sputum cultures (an admitted patient), so the empiric regimen is a beta lactam plus a macrolide: ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus and common gram negatives, and azithromycin covers atypical organisms.
why_wrong_block:
A. Meropenem is a broad carbapenem kept for hospital acquired pneumonia or risk of Pseudomonas or resistant gram negatives; nothing here suggests those risks.
C. Vancomycin covers MRSA, which is added only with MRSA risk factors (prior MRSA, recent IV antibiotics, severe necrotizing pneumonia); it also misses gram negatives.
D. Oseltamivir treats influenza; a lobar consolidation with productive cough is bacterial pneumonia, and oseltamivir plus azithromycin leaves pneumococcus inadequately covered.
key_concept:
Admitted CAP (non ICU): beta lactam (ceftriaxone) + macrolide (azithromycin), or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.
  • Healthy outpatient: macrolide (or amoxicillin, doxycycline)
  • Comorbid outpatient: respiratory fluoroquinolone, or beta lactam + macrolide
  • HAP: antipseudomonal agent (piperacillin tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem)
  • Add vancomycin only for MRSA risk
exam_pearl: Meropenem or vancomycin become right only when the stem gives hospital acquired infection or resistant organism risk factors.

stem: A 27 years old healthy male presented with right sided weakness. He has significant femur fracture 1 week ago. 2 days ago has pulmonary embolism. Brain imaging shows left cerebral infarction. Which of the following is the most likely the cause of his presentation?
why_right: A young, healthy man with a recent femur fracture and pulmonary embolism 2 days ago now has a left cerebral infarct. A venous clot reaching the arterial circulation implies a right to left shunt: this is paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale, made more likely when PE raises right sided pressures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Atrial fibrillation: the commonest cardioembolic cause in older patients, but nothing suggests AF in a healthy 27 year old, and it does not explain the venous thrombus link.
B. Carotid artery stenosis: an atherosclerotic cause in older patients with vascular risk factors (smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia), not a healthy young man.
D. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: presents with exertional syncope, murmur or sudden death in young people; stroke is uncommon and the DVT/PE story points elsewhere.
key_concept:
Venous thrombus + arterial stroke = paradoxical embolism via a right to left shunt.
  • Typical setting: DVT/PE (fracture, immobilization) in a young patient
  • Most common shunt: patent foramen ovale
  • Workup: echocardiography with bubble study
  • Older patient + irregular pulse: think AF
  • Older patient + vascular risk: carotid stenosis
exam_pearl: Young stroke after DVT/PE = PFO; do not reflexively answer AF in a healthy young patient.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with sudden left eye visual loss for 20 minutes. The vision returned to normal after this episode. History reveals, she has diabetes mellitus. The physical examination is normal. Blood pressure 125/75 mmHg, Heart rate 75 /min, Respiratory rate 16/min, Temperature 37.2° C. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: sudden left eye visual loss for 20 minutes
why_right: Sudden monocular visual loss lasting 20 minutes with full recovery in a diabetic is amaurosis fugax, a transient ischemic attack of the retinal circulation (usually emboli from the carotid). Normal examination after the episode fits a TIA because the deficit resolved completely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Multiple sclerosis: optic neuritis in a younger woman develops over days, is often painful on eye movement, and recovers over weeks, not in 20 minutes.
B. Retinal detachment: flashes, floaters and a curtain like field loss that persists and needs urgent surgery; it does not resolve spontaneously.
C. Conversion disorder: a diagnosis of exclusion with psychological triggers; an abrupt, fully resolving vascular type event in a diabetic must be treated as a TIA.
key_concept:
Transient monocular blindness = amaurosis fugax = retinal TIA.
  • Cause: usually carotid emboli
  • Next step: carotid duplex ultrasound
  • Persistent painless loss: central retinal artery occlusion
  • Painful, over days, young woman: optic neuritis (MS)
  • Flashes, floaters, curtain: retinal detachment
exam_pearl: Resolved within minutes plus vascular risk factor = TIA; a deficit that persists is a different diagnosis.

stem: A 43-year-old man comes to the clinic for a follow-up. He has been recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and has been following a plan of lifestyle measures to improve his diet and increase his level of exercise (see lab result). Blood pressure 129/80 mmHg, BMI 32 kg/m2. Test Result Normal Values: HA1C 6.9 4.7-5.6 %. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment option now?
why_right: He was recently diagnosed and has already completed a lifestyle plan, yet his HbA1c is still 6.9% with BMI 32. After a 3 to 6 month lifestyle trial, an HbA1c still above 6.5% means lifestyle alone has failed, so metformin is started: it is the first line drug, weight neutral, does not cause hypoglycemia, and suits obese patients.
why_wrong_block:
A. Insulin: started when HbA1c is very high (above 10%) or the patient is catabolic/symptomatic; not for an HbA1c of 6.9%.
C. Sulphonylurea: a second line add on (or for intolerance to metformin); causes weight gain and hypoglycemia, a poor first choice in obesity.
D. Further diet and exercise: appropriate as the first trial at diagnosis, but he has already done this and is still above target, so drug therapy is now needed.
key_concept:
T2DM first step by HbA1c.
  • Below 7.5% at diagnosis: lifestyle for 3 to 6 months, then metformin if HbA1c still above 6.5%
  • 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle + metformin
  • Above 10% or symptomatic catabolism: insulin
  • Metformin avoided if eGFR below 30
  • Usual long term target: HbA1c below 7%
exam_pearl: The lead-in word 'now' after a completed lifestyle trial means escalate to metformin, not more lifestyle.

stem: A 40-year-old man presented with several months history of dyspepsia. He denies any history of dysphagia, vomiting, or weight lost. He has no significant past medical history and not on any medications. He received helicopter pylori eradication (PPI standard dose, clarithromycin 500mg, and amoxil 1g bid for 10 days) with partial response. Basic routine lab was normal (see reports). Endoscopy: Showed gastric erosions. Biopsy: Showed h pylori organism. Which of the following is the best treatment regimen?
OptA: Repeat the same regimen for a longer duration 14 days
OptB: PPI, nitromidazole 500mg bid, doxacyclin 100mg qid for 14 days
OptC: PPI, levofloxacin 500mg gid, amoxil 1 g bid, nitromidazole 500mg bid for 14 days
OptD: PPI, bismuthsubcitrate 300mg qid, tertacycline 500mg id , metronidazole 500mg tid for 14 days
why_right: He received standard clarithromycin based triple therapy, had only a partial response, and a biopsy still shows H. pylori: this is eradication failure. The next regimen should avoid clarithromycin (likely resistance), and bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole for 14 days) is the standard rescue option.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeating the same regimen longer: clarithromycin resistance is the likely reason for failure, so reusing it is not recommended.
B. PPI + metronidazole + doxycycline without bismuth: not a validated eradication regimen; doxycycline is not a substitute for tetracycline here.
C. Levofloxacin based therapy is an alternative rescue (classically PPI + levofloxacin + amoxicillin), but this listed four drug combination is non standard, and bismuth quadruple is the preferred choice offered.
key_concept:
H. pylori treatment ladder.
  • First line: PPI + clarithromycin + amoxicillin (or metronidazole if penicillin allergic)
  • Failure: bismuth quadruple (PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole) for 14 days
  • Alternative rescue: levofloxacin based triple
  • Confirm eradication: urea breath or stool antigen test, off PPI
exam_pearl: After clarithromycin triple therapy fails, never repeat clarithromycin; switch to bismuth quadruple.

stem: A 40-year-old man with Gastro Esophageal Reflux Disease presents to the general physician with 3-month history of intermittent retrosternal burning pain, worse on bending, nausea, regurgitation with an unpleasant taste in the mouth, and a nocturnal cough. The patient has been using over the counter antacids with no relief. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
highlight_terms_source: over the counter antacids with no relief
why_right: Known GERD with 3 months of typical (retrosternal burning worse on bending, regurgitation) and atypical (nocturnal cough) symptoms that failed over the counter antacids needs effective acid suppression. A PPI is the mainstay of GERD treatment and is the most appropriate course now, with lifestyle advice alongside.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgery (fundoplication): reserved for GERD refractory to optimal PPI therapy or with complications; he has not had a PPI yet.
B. Antibiotic: used for H. pylori eradication in peptic ulcer or gastritis, not for reflux symptoms.
C. Lifestyle modification: part of initial management, but alone it is insufficient for persistent symptoms already unresponsive to antacids.
key_concept:
GERD ladder.
  • Typical: heartburn, regurgitation; atypical: nocturnal cough, hoarseness
  • Start: lifestyle advice ± antacids
  • Persistent symptoms: PPI
  • Alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, age above 60, bleeding): endoscopy
  • Refractory to PPI: investigate, then consider fundoplication
exam_pearl: 'Lifestyle modification' is the initial answer only when no treatment has been tried; after failed antacids pick the PPI.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain, bloating and weight loss. Physical examination is unremarkable except for BMI 18% (see lab results and report). Test Result Normal Values: Hb 90 130-170 g/L (Male), 120-160 g/L (Female); MCV 70 80-95 fl; Calcium 2.05 2.15-2.62 mol/L; Phosphate, inorganic 0.79 0.82-1.51 mmol/L; Tissue transglutaminase antibody: Positive. Which of the following is the best management?
why_right: Malabsorption features (abdominal pain, bloating, weight loss, low BMI), microcytic anemia (Hb 90, MCV 70) from iron malabsorption, low calcium and phosphate, and a positive tissue transglutaminase antibody indicate celiac disease. The treatment is a lifelong strict gluten free diet.
why_wrong_block:
A. Glucocorticoids: used in refractory celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease flares, not as first line for celiac disease.
C. Metronidazole: treats giardiasis, C. difficile or small bowel bacterial overgrowth; serology here points to celiac disease.
D. Ciprofloxacin: for bacterial enteric infections such as traveller's diarrhea; a chronic malabsorptive picture with positive tTG is not infective.
key_concept:
Celiac disease.
  • Clues: diarrhea/bloating, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, low calcium/vitamin D
  • Screen: anti tTG IgA (check total IgA)
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy) while on gluten
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten free diet
  • Follow compliance: falling tTG titre
exam_pearl: Iron deficiency anemia in a young adult with no blood loss plus malabsorption = think celiac.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents to Emergency Department with altered sensorium. He was recently diagnosed to have inoperable small cell carcinoma of the lung. On examination, he is euvolemic (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 76 /min. Test Result Normal Values: Sodium 115 134-146 mmol/L; Potassium 3.8 3.5-5.1 mmol/L; Urea 4.3 2.75-7.4 mmol/L; Creatinine 76 44-115 mol/L. Which of the following is the best initial management?
highlight_terms_source: small cell carcinoma of the lung
why_right: Small cell lung cancer, euvolemia and Na 115 point to SIADH, but the decisive clue is altered sensorium: this is severe symptomatic hyponatremia. The best initial management is hypertonic (3%) saline to raise sodium promptly, with a limited rate of correction to avoid osmotic demyelination; fluid restriction is for asymptomatic SIADH.
why_wrong_block:
A. 5% dextrose: free water once the glucose is metabolized, which would lower sodium further and worsen cerebral edema.
B. Normal saline: correct for hypovolemic hyponatremia; in SIADH the salt is excreted and water retained, so sodium may fall further.
D. Half normal saline: hypotonic, so it worsens hyponatremia; used in hypernatremia or after initial resuscitation in DKA.
key_concept:
Hyponatremia by volume status and symptoms.
  • Severe symptoms (confusion, seizures, coma): hypertonic 3% saline
  • Hypovolemic: 0.9% saline
  • Euvolemic (SIADH) without severe symptoms: fluid restriction
  • Hypervolemic: fluid restriction + loop diuretic
  • Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination
exam_pearl: Symptoms trump cause: SIADH is treated with fluid restriction, unless the patient is neurologically symptomatic.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of breathlessness. He has been smoking all his adult life, he smokes 10-15 cigarettes per day. On examination, he has lost the nail fold angle of his fingers. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Loss of the nail fold angle is finger clubbing. In a lifelong smoker with 6 months of breathlessness, new clubbing should be assumed to be bronchial carcinoma until proven otherwise, because COPD and asthma never cause clubbing and aspergillosis does not typically present this way.
why_wrong_block:
A. COPD: the commonest cause of breathlessness in smokers, but it does not cause clubbing; clubbing in a COPD patient should prompt a search for lung cancer.
C. Aspergillosis: ABPA presents in asthmatics with wheeze and eosinophilia, aspergilloma with hemoptysis in an old cavity; clubbing is not the key feature.
D. Asthma: episodic wheeze and cough with atopy, usually starting younger; it never causes clubbing.
key_concept:
Clubbing = look for a cause; it is never COPD or asthma alone.
  • Lung: bronchial carcinoma, bronchiectasis, lung abscess/empyema, cystic fibrosis, pulmonary fibrosis
  • Cardiac: cyanotic congenital heart disease, infective endocarditis
  • GI: inflammatory bowel disease, cirrhosis, celiac disease
exam_pearl: Smoker + breathlessness alone = COPD; smoker + clubbing = bronchial carcinoma.

stem: A 60-year-old man with a history of 20-pack-year smoking presents with exertional dyspnea and productive cough for 3 months. He had similar attack last year. On examination, he has central cyanosis and expiratory wheeze on lung auscultation (see lab results). Test Result Normal Values: ABG HCO3- 36 22-28 mmol/L; ABG PCO2 7.7 4.7-6.0 kPa; pH 7.35 7.36-7.45; ABG PO2 8.4 10.6-14.2 kPa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: "Productive cough for 3 months" with a "similar attack last year" in a 20 pack-year smoker is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis (productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years). Central cyanosis plus wheeze is the "blue bloater" picture, and the ABG shows CO2 retention (PCO2 7.7 kPa) with a raised HCO3 of 36 and near-normal pH 7.35: a chronic, metabolically compensated respiratory acidosis typical of COPD.
why_wrong_block:
A. Asthma is episodic and reversible, usually starts younger, and does not produce chronic CO2 retention with a compensatory high bicarbonate. Right when: variable wheeze with triggers and a big bronchodilator response.
C. PE is acute and causes hypoxia with LOW PCO2 from hyperventilation, not a 3 month productive cough recurring yearly. Right when: sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, DVT risk.
D. Interstitial fibrosis gives a dry cough, fine "Velcro" inspiratory crackles, clubbing and a restrictive pattern with type 1 failure (normal or low PCO2), not wheeze and CO2 retention.
key_concept:
Smoker + productive cough ≥3 months in 2 consecutive years = chronic bronchitis.
  • High PCO2 + high HCO3 + near-normal pH = chronic compensated respiratory acidosis (CO2 retainer)
  • Blue bloater: cyanosis, cough, CO2 retention (chronic bronchitis)
  • PE: low PCO2
  • ILD: dry cough, Velcro crackles, restrictive, type 1 failure
exam_pearl: A raised HCO3 with a high PCO2 tells you the CO2 retention is chronic: think COPD, not an acute event.

stem: A 60-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for cardiac risk assessment. He is asymptomatic and physically active. He has never smoked. He has no chronic health issues and takes no medications. His physical examinations are normal. Cardiovascular risk calculation using the Pooled Cohort Equations predicts a 6.5% risk of a myocardial infarction in the next 10 years that indicate an intermediate risk of myocardial infarction. Which of the following investigations should be done next?
why_right: The patient is "asymptomatic" and the Pooled Cohort Equations place him at "intermediate risk", so the question is how to refine his risk to decide on a statin, not how to look for ischemia. High-sensitivity CRP is a risk-enhancing marker that, added to the calculated risk, helps tip the decision toward statin therapy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coronary CT angiography is anatomic imaging for symptomatic patients with suspected coronary disease, not risk refinement in someone without symptoms.
B. Stress echo looks for inducible ischemia and is indicated for symptoms suggesting angina; it is not a screening test in asymptomatic people.
D. CMR evaluates cardiac structure, function and tissue (cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, viability); it has no role in primary prevention risk refinement.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic + intermediate ASCVD risk: refine risk to guide statin, do not image for ischemia.
  • Risk enhancers: hs-CRP, family history of premature ASCVD, Lp(a), ApoB, ABI, CKD, metabolic syndrome
  • If imaging is used for refinement it is a non-contrast coronary calcium score, not CT angiography
  • Symptoms suggesting ischemia: stress testing or CCTA
exam_pearl: "Asymptomatic" in the stem rules out every ischemia or anatomy test; pick the risk-refining marker.

stem: A 68-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnea and dry cough for 7 days. His medical history is significant for hypertension. Physical examination reveals raised central venous pressure, fine crackles at lung bases and hepatomegaly. His extremity examination reveals bilateral pitting edema. Echocardiogram shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% and normal valves. Chest radiograph shows evidence of pulmonary edema (see lab results). Blood pressure 160/85 mmHg, Heart rate 86 /min, Respiratory rate 18 /min. Test Result Normal Values: Sodium 140 134-146 mmol/L; Potassium 4 3.5-5.1 mmol/L; Urea 6 2.75-7.4 mmol/L; Creatinine 88 44-115 mol/L; Brain natriuretic peptide 900 0-300 ng/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: Orthopnea, raised CVP, basal crackles, hepatomegaly, pitting edema, pulmonary edema on CXR and BNP 900 mean acute decompensated heart failure with congestion. The preserved EF (60%, normal valves) in a hypertensive man makes it HFpEF, but that does not change the acute step: relieve congestion with a loop diuretic (furosemide).
why_wrong_block:
A. Calcium channel blockers do not relieve fluid overload, and non-dihydropyridines are negatively inotropic. They may help long-term BP control, not acute congestion.
B. Beta-blockers are not started during acute decompensation; they are introduced once the patient is euvolemic and stable (mainly for HFrEF).
C. Spironolactone is long-term prognostic therapy, with a weak and slow diuretic effect; it is not the immediate treatment for pulmonary edema.
key_concept:
ADHF with congestion: IV loop diuretic first, regardless of EF.
  • Clues: orthopnea, raised JVP, crackles, edema, hepatomegaly, high BNP
  • HFpEF: diuretics for congestion + control BP and comorbidities
  • Do not START beta-blockers in decompensation
  • MRA and beta-blockers = chronic prognostic therapy
exam_pearl: A normal EF does not exclude heart failure: congestion signs plus high BNP still mean furosemide.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presented to the clinic with 2-months history of polyarthralgia, skin rash, mucosal ulcers and fatigue. Her clinical examinations revealed malar rash over her face and active arthritis at several joints (see lab results). Hb 100 (130-170 g/L male; 120-160 g/L female); Platelets count 100 (150-400 x 10^9/L); WBC 3 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L); ESR 35; Lupus anticoagulant positive (negative); Urea 5; Creatinine 78; C-reactive peptide 5 (<8.2 mg/L); Complement C3 0.3 (0.7-1.5 g/L); Complement C4 0.13 (0.15-0.45 g/L). Which of the following test obtained at this visit is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key is ANA. The young woman has a classic SLE picture: malar rash, mucosal ulcers, arthritis, pancytopenia, low C3/C4 and a positive lupus anticoagulant. ANA is positive in nearly all SLE patients, so it is the test used to establish the autoimmune basis; a negative ANA practically excludes SLE.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anti-Ro (SSA) is linked to Sjögren syndrome, subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus/congenital heart block; it is not the test that confirms systemic lupus.
C. Anti-dsDNA is highly specific for SLE and tracks disease activity and nephritis, but it is negative in a sizeable share of patients, so it cannot exclude lupus; this recall keys the sensitive test, ANA.
D. Anti-RNP confirms mixed connective tissue disease (SLE features overlapping with myositis, Raynaud, scleroderma); there is no myositis or overlap here.
key_concept:
SLE antibodies: ANA most sensitive, anti-Sm and anti-dsDNA most specific.
  • ANA: most sensitive, screening; negative ANA practically excludes SLE
  • Anti-Sm: most specific
  • Anti-dsDNA: specific, activity and nephritis
  • Low C3/C4: activity, nephritis
  • Anti-histone: drug-induced lupus
  • Anti-Ro/La: neonatal lupus, Sjögren
exam_pearl: "Most sensitive / screening" = ANA; "most specific" = anti-Sm (then anti-dsDNA); SLE plus myositis overlap = anti-RNP.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed version: 'Long case with classic presentation of SLE. Asking what is most important initial serology test? A- Anti-ccp, B- ANA, B- Anti-dsDna, C- Antiphospholipid. Answer: B (ANA).' Fuller screenshot version (top of next page) marks ** B. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

stem: Radiation exposure After 2 wks , abdominal pain loss of appetite and genralize fatigue
why_right: After significant radiation exposure the bone marrow is the most radiosensitive organ, and the hematopoietic syndrome declares itself after a latent period, with counts falling over the following weeks. Symptoms appearing "after 2 wks" such as generalized fatigue, anorexia and abdominal discomfort fit bone marrow destruction (anemia, neutropenia with infection, thrombocytopenia), rather than an immediate or a late effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anaphylactic shock is an immediate IgE-mediated reaction to an allergen (minutes), with hypotension, urticaria and bronchospasm; radiation does not cause it and the timing is 2 weeks.
B. Radiation-induced malignancy (leukemia, thyroid, solid tumors) is a late effect appearing years later, not 2 weeks after exposure.
key_concept:
Acute radiation syndrome: prodrome, latent phase, then organ syndrome by dose.
  • Hematopoietic: lowest dose; pancytopenia over weeks (fatigue, infection, bleeding)
  • Gastrointestinal: higher dose; vomiting, diarrhea, GI bleeding
  • Neurovascular: very high dose; rapid collapse, fatal
  • Malignancy: late effect, years later
exam_pearl: Timing decides: minutes = allergy, weeks = marrow failure, years = cancer.

stem: Pt with left-sided sensorineural hearing loss and left-sided facial weakness
why_right: The labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery usually arises from the AICA, and the AICA also supplies the lateral inferior pons where the facial nucleus and nerve lie. So an AICA infarct gives ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss plus ipsilateral facial weakness (CN VIII + CN VII), often with vertigo and ataxia, exactly the "left-sided hearing loss and left-sided facial weakness" here.
why_wrong_block:
A. Not a standard posterior circulation vessel; if the superior cerebellar artery is intended, it causes ipsilateral limb ataxia and contralateral pain and temperature loss, without hearing loss or facial palsy.
B. MCA stroke gives CONTRALATERAL face and arm weakness (upper motor neuron, forehead spared), sensory loss and aphasia or neglect; it does not cause hearing loss.
key_concept:
Brainstem strokes: ipsilateral cranial nerve signs + crossed long tract signs.
  • AICA (lateral pontine): ipsilateral deafness (CN VIII) + facial palsy (CN VII), vertigo, ataxia
  • PICA (lateral medullary, Wallenberg): dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain/temperature loss, Horner
  • SCA: ipsilateral ataxia
  • MCA: contralateral face/arm weakness, aphasia
exam_pearl: Hearing loss in a stroke points to AICA, because the labyrinthine artery comes off it.
compiler_note: Compiler note: AICA syndrome responsible for both CN VII and CN VIII palsies. (Screenshot originally numbered 388.)

stem: Adult patient presented with meningitis. No Na mentioned. Most likely causative organism?
why_right: This recall's key is Listeria monocytogenes, which is the organism to name when an adult with meningitis has a Listeria risk factor: age over 50, pregnancy, immunosuppression (steroids, transplant, malignancy), diabetes or alcoholism. The recall has lost most of its stem detail ("No Na mentioned"), so the original question likely contained one of these clues; Listeria is also why ampicillin is added to empirical cover in those groups.
why_wrong_block:
A. Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of bacterial meningitis in adults overall; it is the answer for a previously well adult without Listeria risk factors.
C. Staphylococcal meningitis follows neurosurgery, shunts, penetrating head trauma or bacteremia from endocarditis, not typical community-acquired meningitis.
D. E. coli is a neonatal meningitis organism (with group B strep and Listeria) or follows neurosurgery; it is not typical in community adults.
key_concept:
Meningitis organism by host:
  • Neonate: group B strep, E. coli, Listeria
  • Adult (most common overall): S. pneumoniae; young adults: also N. meningitidis
  • Over 50, pregnant, immunocompromised, alcoholic: add Listeria (cover with ampicillin)
  • Post-neurosurgery or shunt: Staphylococcus, Gram negatives
exam_pearl: No risk factor in an adult = pneumococcus; age over 50, pregnancy or immunosuppression is what turns the answer to Listeria.

stem: Best antihypertensive medication after TIA?
why_right: For secondary prevention "after TIA" or stroke, BP lowering with an ACE inhibitor (often combined with a thiazide-like diuretic) has trial evidence for reducing recurrent stroke, so ramipril is the preferred choice. ACE inhibitors also protect the kidney and heart in the many TIA patients who have diabetes or vascular disease.
why_wrong_block: A. Beta-blockers such as metoprolol are less effective at preventing stroke than other classes and are not first line for hypertension after TIA; use them when there is another indication (angina, post-MI, HFrEF, rate control in AF).
key_concept:
Antihypertensive choice by indication:
  • After TIA/stroke: ACE inhibitor ± thiazide-like diuretic
  • Diabetes or CKD with proteinuria: ACE inhibitor/ARB
  • Post-MI, angina, HFrEF: beta-blocker added
  • Beta-blockers: weakest for stroke prevention
exam_pearl: Beta-blockers are the trap: good for the heart, poor for stroke prevention.

stem: Patient with cervical lymphadenopathy, and hepatomegaly. chest xray hilar lymphadenopathy, mass in the mid section? Of the lung. Best biopsy option?
key_concept:
Biopsy the least invasive site that gives tissue diagnosis and staging.
  • Palpable peripheral node (cervical, supraclavicular): easiest target if offered
  • Hilar/mediastinal nodes or central mass: bronchoscopy with transbronchial or EBUS-guided sampling
  • Peripheral lung lesion: CT-guided transthoracic biopsy
  • Pleural effusion: thoracentesis then pleural biopsy
  • Liver: only for focal lesions when no easier site
exam_pearl: Hilar lymphadenopathy is reached through the airway; the pleura is only biopsied when the pleura is involved.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Female stopped smoking 20 years ago. Incidental asymptomatic 1 cm pulmonary nodule found. Most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Solitary pulmonary nodule by size:
  • ≤4 mm: no routine follow-up in low risk
  • More than 4 to 8 mm: CT follow-up at 3 to 6 months
  • More than 8 mm to 2 cm: PET/CT, then biopsy if suspicious (CT at 3 months is an option if low risk)
  • Over 2 cm: baseline PFT then surgery
  • A companion recall of this same scenario is keyed to follow-up CT
exam_pearl: 1 cm sits just above the 8 mm line, so check whether the stem's risk level pushes you to surveillance or to tissue.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer printed; see 2062 (same scenario, Answer A: Follow-up CT).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 55-year-old woman is referred to the clinic because of a 1 cm solitary nodule with sharp borders in the right lung. The nodule was detected on an abdominal CT performed to evaluate abdominal pain. She does not have any respiratory complaints. She smoked 20 cigarettes per day for 10 years but managed to stop smoking 20 years ago. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: 1 cm solitary nodule with sharp borders
why_right: An incidental, asymptomatic, 1 cm solid nodule with sharp (smooth) borders in a woman who quit smoking 20 years ago carries a low to intermediate malignancy risk. Smooth margins favour a benign lesion, so the key here is surveillance with a repeat CT at about 3 to 6 months to document stability or growth before any invasive step.
why_wrong_block:
B. A 1 cm nodule in a former smoker cannot simply be discharged. No follow-up is reserved for very small, low-risk nodules (the threshold is about 4 to 6 mm depending on the guideline version).
C. Biopsy is invasive and is chosen when the nodule looks suspicious (spiculated, growing, or PET-avid). A small peripheral nodule also gives a low transbronchial yield.
D. Resection is for nodules that are highly suspicious, proven malignant, or large (over 2 cm in the size ladder). A smooth 1 cm nodule does not justify surgery first.
key_concept:
Solitary pulmonary nodule: decide by size, morphology and smoking risk.
  • ≤4 mm, low risk: no follow-up
  • >4 to 8 mm: serial CT surveillance
  • >8 mm: CT at about 3 months, PET/CT, or tissue sampling depending on risk
  • >2 cm or clearly malignant: baseline PFT then surgery
  • Smooth borders, calcification, stability for 2 years: benign features
  • Spiculation, growth, upper lobe, heavy smoking: malignant features
exam_pearl: Old CXR available? Compare first: a nodule stable for years needs no further work-up.

stem: Alcoholic patient with recurrent epigastric pain and multiple admissions. Mildly elevated amylase. Most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The decisive clues are alcoholic, recurrent epigastric pain and multiple admissions: repeated bouts of alcohol-related pancreatic inflammation lead to chronic pancreatitis. Only a mildly elevated amylase fits, because the fibrosed gland has lost much of its acinar tissue and can no longer produce the marked enzyme rise seen in an acute attack.
why_wrong_block:
A. Biliary colic: brief, self-limiting pain after fatty meals in a patient with gallstones, with normal enzymes; nothing here points to gallstones and alcohol is the risk factor given.
C. Acute cholecystitis: a single episode of constant RUQ pain with fever, Murphy sign and leukocytosis; it does not explain years of recurrent admissions linked to alcohol.
key_concept:
Recurrent alcohol-related epigastric pain + only mild enzyme rise = chronic pancreatitis.
  • Acute pancreatitis: amylase or lipase ≥3 times normal, pain radiating to the back
  • Chronic pancreatitis: enzymes normal or mildly raised (burnt-out gland)
  • Late triad: chronic pain, steatorrhoea (exocrine failure), diabetes (endocrine failure)
  • Imaging: pancreatic calcification on CT
  • Alcohol is the commonest cause in adults
exam_pearl: A high amylase points to an acute attack; a low or mildly raised amylase does not exclude pancreatitis when the history is chronic.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Source lettered the third option 'D'.

stem: Patient on warfarin for DVT has INR 6 but no bleeding. Management in addition to withholding warfarin
why_right: The patient has INR 6 with no bleeding, which falls in the INR 4 to 10 non-bleeding band. Here the warfarin is held for a dose or two and the INR is rechecked closely, so repeat INR in 2 days is correct; reversal agents are not needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vitamin K: routine oral vitamin K is given when the INR is above 10 without bleeding; at INR 4 to 10 it is only considered in patients at high bleeding risk.
B. Fresh frozen plasma: reserved for a patient who is bleeding (given with IV vitamin K in hospital); this patient is not bleeding.
C. Cryoprecipitate: replaces fibrinogen and does not supply the vitamin K dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X), so it does not reverse warfarin.
key_concept:
High INR on warfarin: first ask, is the patient bleeding?
  • No bleeding, INR above target but below 10: hold warfarin, recheck INR
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin plus oral vitamin K
  • Bleeding: admit, IV vitamin K plus PCC or FFP
  • Restart warfarin once INR back in range
exam_pearl: The word "bleeding" or an INR above 10 is what moves the answer from rechecking INR to vitamin K or factor replacement.

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents to the follow-up clinic. She is known to have idiopathic deep venous thrombosis and is on warfarin, which was initiated 6 weeks ago. The examination is unremarkable (see lab result). Which of the following is the most appropriate management in addition to withholding warfarin?
why_right: A "follow-up clinic" visit with an "unremarkable" examination means she is not bleeding, and the keyed answer implies a supratherapeutic INR in the 4 to 10 range. For a non-bleeding patient in that range, the algorithm is to hold warfarin and arrange close follow-up, so re-measuring the INR in 2 days is the right addition. Vitamin K is only considered here, mainly in patients at high bleeding risk.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vitamin K is routinely given only when the INR is above 10 without bleeding (oral) or with any bleeding (IV); for INR 4 to 10 it is merely considered in high bleeding risk.
C. FFP is for warfarin patients with active bleeding who are admitted, combined with IV vitamin K; she is not bleeding.
D. PCC gives rapid reversal for significant or life threatening bleeding on warfarin; it is not used for a raised INR in a stable outpatient.
key_concept:
High INR on warfarin: first ask, is the patient bleeding?
  • No bleeding, INR 4 to 10: hold warfarin, recheck INR, consider oral vitamin K 1 to 2.5 mg
  • No bleeding, INR above 10: hold warfarin + oral vitamin K 2.5 to 5 mg
  • Any bleeding: admit, IV vitamin K 10 mg + FFP or PCC
  • Clinic visit + normal exam = no bleeding
exam_pearl: Bleeding, not the INR number, is what moves you to FFP or PCC.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Lab result referenced in stem is not shown on the page.

stem: Patient presented with obvious UTI symptoms. Urinalysis showed positive nitrites and hematuria. Most appropriate management?
why_right: Obvious UTI symptoms with positive nitrites on urinalysis make bacterial cystitis very likely, so antibiotics are started empirically. Hematuria is common in cystitis and does not change management. Culture is not required before treating simple uncomplicated cystitis.
why_wrong_block: B. Urine culture only: delays treatment of a symptomatic infection; culture is added (alongside, not instead of, treatment) in pyelonephritis, pregnancy, men, recurrent or complicated UTI, or treatment failure.
key_concept:
Symptomatic uncomplicated cystitis + positive dipstick = empiric antibiotics.
  • Nitrites and leukocyte esterase are the dipstick markers of UTI
  • Culture: pregnancy, pyelonephritis, structural abnormality, recurrence or failure
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy (or before urological procedures)
exam_pearl: Do not wait for culture in a symptomatic woman with positive nitrites; waiting is right only for asymptomatic findings outside pregnancy.

stem: Which of the following findings is most characteristic of nephrotic syndrome?
why_right: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema (usually with hyperlipidaemia). Of the options, low serum albumin is the only one that is part of the diagnostic definition, because massive urinary protein loss drains plasma albumin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hematuria: a hallmark of nephritic syndrome (inflammatory glomerular injury); it is not required for nephrotic syndrome and is usually absent in minimal change disease.
B. Hypertension: characteristic of nephritic syndrome with salt and water retention; it may occur in nephrotic syndrome but is not a diagnostic feature.
key_concept:
Nephrotic vs nephritic.
  • Nephrotic: proteinuria above 3.5 g/day, low albumin, oedema, hyperlipidaemia
  • Nephritic: hematuria (RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria, raised creatinine
  • Child with puffy eyes and 4+ protein: serum albumin confirms the diagnosis
exam_pearl: Hematuria and hypertension push the answer to nephritic syndrome; low albumin and heavy proteinuria keep it nephrotic.

stem: A patient with diabetic and hypertension is found to have persistent proteinuria. Which antihypertensive medication is preferred?
why_right: Diabetes with persistent proteinuria indicates diabetic nephropathy, so the preferred antihypertensive is a RAAS blocker. An ACE inhibitor dilates the efferent arteriole, lowers intraglomerular pressure, reduces proteinuria and slows progression of kidney disease, beyond its effect on blood pressure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Calcium channel blocker: lowers BP and is a good add-on, but it does not reduce proteinuria the way RAAS blockade does; first choice in older non-diabetic patients without proteinuria.
C. Thiazide diuretic: effective for BP and useful as an add-on, but it gives no specific renoprotection in diabetic nephropathy.
D. Beta blocker: not first line for uncomplicated hypertension and not renoprotective; chosen when there is another indication such as post-MI, angina or heart failure.
key_concept:
Hypertension + diabetes or proteinuric CKD = ACE inhibitor (or ARB).
  • ACE inhibitor cough: switch to ARB
  • Do not combine ACE inhibitor with ARB
  • Check creatinine and potassium after starting
  • Contraindicated in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis
exam_pearl: If the stem adds "developed a dry cough on enalapril", the answer becomes an ARB, not a different class.

stem: A patient came complaining of epigastric pain with burning sensation, which of the following do you advice him to do;
OptC: Decrease frequency of meals (smth like that)
why_right: Burning epigastric pain suggests acid reflux or dyspepsia, and the question asks for lifestyle advice. Avoiding lying down after eating uses gravity to keep gastric contents out of the oesophagus and is a standard reflux measure, together with raising the head of the bed and avoiding late meals.
why_wrong_block:
B. Avoid eating 30 mins before bedtime: the interval is far too short; the usual advice is to stop eating about 2 to 3 hours before lying down for the night.
C. Decrease frequency of meals: fewer meals means larger meals, which distend the stomach and worsen reflux; patients are advised to eat smaller, more frequent meals.
D. Avoid ginger: ginger is not one of the recognised reflux triggers; patients are told to limit fatty food, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, mint, spicy food and smoking.
key_concept:
GERD lifestyle measures.
  • Do not lie down after meals; last meal 2 to 3 hours before bed
  • Elevate the head of the bed
  • Small frequent meals rather than large ones
  • Weight loss if overweight; stop smoking
  • Limit fat, chocolate, caffeine, alcohol, mint
  • Persistent symptoms: PPI trial; alarm features: endoscopy
exam_pearl: Watch the timing: "30 minutes before bed" is a distractor; the protective gap is hours, not minutes.

stem: obese woman w bp 152/90 + renal bruit on examination. what to do?
key_concept:
Suspected renal artery stenosis (bruit, resistant or new hypertension, rise in creatinine on ACE inhibitor).
  • Screening: duplex Doppler ultrasound
  • Non-invasive confirmation: CT angiography or MR angiography
  • Gold standard: catheter renal angiography
  • Young woman: fibromuscular dysplasia; older vascular patient: atherosclerosis
exam_pearl: The lead-in decides it: "initial" favours Doppler ultrasound, "most appropriate" or "most accurate" favours CT angiography.

⚠ Image audit: Page says only 'The Stem Was Most Appropriate, Answer Is CT'; two options contain CT (pelvic/abdomen CT and renal CT), so the endorsed option cannot be pinned to B.

stem: question about someone with SLE, which drug should be modified:
key_concept:
Drug review in SLE.
  • APS on warfarin and pregnant: switch to LMWH plus low-dose aspirin
  • Hydroxychloroquine: continue in pregnancy and lactation
  • Lupus nephritis with proteinuria: ACE inhibitor or ARB for BP
  • Drug-induced lupus: hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid; stop the culprit
exam_pearl: If the stem mentions pregnancy, the drug to change is almost always the teratogen (warfarin).

stem: Adult asthmatic patient has recurrent cough and wheeze when exposed to dust and perfumes. On physical examination, she has mild respiratory wheeze that failed to respond to albuterol. Spirometry shows a reversible obstructive pattern. What is the next step in management?
why_right: Spirometry with a reversible obstructive pattern confirms asthma, and her symptoms are recurrent and have failed to respond to albuterol. Asthma not controlled on a reliever alone needs a controller, so the next step is to add an inhaled corticosteroid such as budesonide.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inhaled salbutamol: this is the same drug as albuterol, which has already failed; SABA alone is the starting step only when symptoms are purely occasional and controlled.
C. Inhaled ipratropium: a short-acting antimuscarinic used mainly as an add-on in acute exacerbations or in COPD, not as asthma maintenance.
D. Montelukast: an alternative or add-on controller when ICS cannot be used or control is still poor on ICS; ICS remains the preferred first controller.
key_concept:
Asthma step-up.
  • Occasional trigger-only symptoms: as-needed reliever
  • Uncontrolled on reliever alone: add ICS (budesonide)
  • Still uncontrolled: ICS plus LABA (e.g. budesonide/formoterol)
  • Further steps: higher-dose ICS, add-ons (LTRA, LAMA), then oral steroids or biologics
  • Check inhaler technique and adherence before stepping up
exam_pearl: The same dust/perfume stem without "failed to respond to albuterol" is keyed to salbutamol; the failed reliever is what moves the answer to ICS.

stem: ECG absent p wave with hx of stroke
why_right: Absent P waves with an irregularly irregular baseline is the ECG signature of atrial fibrillation: the atria fibrillate chaotically, so no organized atrial depolarization (P wave) is seen. The history of stroke fits too, because stasis in the fibrillating left atrial appendage forms thrombi that embolize to the brain, which is why AF patients are risk scored (CHA2DS2-VASc) for anticoagulation.
why_wrong_block: B. Atrial flutter also lacks normal P waves but shows regular sawtooth flutter waves (best seen in II, III, aVF) with a regular, often 2:1, ventricular response; it also carries stroke risk, but the classic exam pairing of 'absent P waves' is AF.
key_concept:
AF = no P waves + irregularly irregular RR; flutter = sawtooth F waves + regular RR.
  • AF in JVP: absent a waves
  • Main AF complication: thromboembolic stroke
  • CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2: start anticoagulation
  • Prior stroke/TIA scores 2 points
exam_pearl: Regular rhythm with sawtooth baseline flips the answer to atrial flutter; irregularly irregular with no P waves stays AF.

stem:
A 30 years old male came with nausea and vomiting.
Anti-HAV IgM: Negative
HBsAg: positive
HBeAg: positive
Anti-HCV: negative.
What the type of hepatitis causing this ?
why_right: HBsAg positive means active hepatitis B infection, and HBeAg positive means active viral replication with high infectivity. With anti-HAV IgM and anti-HCV both negative, the nausea and vomiting are explained by hepatitis B.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute hepatitis A is diagnosed by anti-HAV IgM, which is negative here.
C. Hepatitis C would need a positive anti-HCV (confirmed by HCV RNA); it is negative here, and HBsAg/HBeAg are hepatitis B markers.
D. Hepatitis D needs HBsAg to exist, but it is diagnosed only with anti-HDV or HDV RNA, which were not tested; positive HBsAg and HBeAg alone point to hepatitis B.
key_concept:
Read the marker that belongs to each virus.
  • HBsAg: active infection (first marker to appear)
  • HBeAg: high replication and infectivity
  • Anti-HBc IgM: acute HBV
  • Anti-HBs alone: vaccination; anti-HBs + anti-HBc: recovered
  • Anti-HAV IgM: acute hepatitis A
  • HDV: only with HBsAg, confirm by anti-HDV
exam_pearl: HBsAg positive does not make it hepatitis D unless anti-HDV is reported positive.

stem: CNS question, MRI. It was hyperintense lesions that's disseminated in place and time. What's the diagnosis?
key_concept:
Dissemination in space and time on MRI = multiple sclerosis. A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Multiple sclerosis.
  • MS: CNS, relapsing, periventricular lesions, oligoclonal bands
  • GBS: PNS, post infectious, ascending weakness, areflexia
  • GBS CSF: high protein, normal cells
exam_pearl: Brain or cord lesions mean CNS (MS); absent reflexes with normal imaging mean PNS (GBS).

Compiler note: No answer marked on the numbered recall. A fuller 'Q:' version at the top of the next page (Answer: A, Multiple Sclerosis) is carded separately.
