stem: 20-Year-Old Female With Transient Vision Loss During Sport, No Other Symptoms, MRI Brain: Multiple Demyelinating Hyperintense Lesion In Periventricular And White Matter Area, What Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Multiple Demyelinating Hyperintense Lesion In Periventricular And White Matter Area
why_right: A 20-year-old female with transient vision loss during sport (heat or exercise worsening of symptoms, Uhthoff phenomenon, suggesting optic nerve demyelination) and MRI showing multiple demyelinating hyperintense periventricular white matter lesions is the classic picture of multiple sclerosis. Young age, female sex and periventricular demyelination are the decisive clues.
why_wrong_block:
B. Primary CNS lymphoma is usually a solitary or few enhancing periventricular masses in older or immunosuppressed patients with progressive deficits, not transient visual symptoms in a healthy young woman.
C. Brain vasculitis gives headache, encephalopathy, multifocal strokes and infarcts in different vascular territories, not demyelinating periventricular lesions with isolated transient vision loss.
D. Neuropsychiatric SLE needs a background of lupus (rash, arthritis, low complement) and presents with seizures, psychosis or cognitive change; none is given here.
key_concept:
Young woman + optic or sensory episode + periventricular demyelinating lesions = MS.
  • Key test: MRI brain and spine (T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions)
  • Supportive: CSF oligoclonal bands
  • Uhthoff: symptoms worse with heat or exercise
  • Acute relapse: high dose IV methylprednisolone
exam_pearl: If the stem gives known SLE with seizures, the same MRI lesions point to neuropsychiatric lupus instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant belonging to 2126 (top of p531).

stem: A 70-year-old woman presents with fatigue and exertional dyspnea for several months. Medical history includes longstanding hypertension and chronic kidney disease, and she is not adherent to her medications. Examination reveals pale mucous membranes and nail beds (see lab results and report). Kidney ultrasonography: Showed small kidneys bilaterally with echographic features suggesting chronic kidney disease. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's anemia?
why_right: Small kidneys bilaterally on ultrasound confirm advanced chronic kidney disease, the end result of her longstanding, poorly controlled hypertension. The renal cortex is the main source of erythropoietin, so loss of renal mass gives a normocytic, normochromic, hypoproliferative anemia; the expected labs show normal MCV with adequate iron stores (normal or high ferritin and TSAT). Erythropoietin deficiency is therefore the most likely cause.
why_wrong_block:
B. Myelodysplastic syndrome: consider in an older patient with macrocytosis, other cytopenias or dysplasia on smear; here the anemia is fully explained by CKD.
C. Iron deficiency: would show low MCV, low ferritin and low TSAT, usually with a blood loss source; the expected labs here show replete iron stores.
D. Inflammation: anemia of chronic inflammation needs an underlying infection, autoimmune disease or cancer; none is present, and the decisive clue is small kidneys.
key_concept:
Anemia of CKD = erythropoietin deficiency.
  • Normocytic, normochromic, low reticulocytes
  • Ferritin and TSAT normal or high
  • Small echogenic kidneys = chronic disease
  • Treatment: replete iron if low, then subcutaneous ESA
  • Hb target on ESA: about 10 to 11.5 g/dL
exam_pearl: Low ferritin/TSAT in a CKD patient means iron deficiency first; replete iron points to EPO deficiency.

stem: Case of thyroiditis after URTI she was anxious and had palpitations ,low iodine uptake what to give now
why_right: Thyroiditis after URTI with low iodine uptake is subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: the thyroid is inflamed and leaking stored hormone, not overproducing it. Her anxiety and palpitations are adrenergic symptoms, so the treatment 'now' is a beta blocker (propranolol), plus NSAIDs or steroids for pain.
why_wrong_block: B. Carbimazole blocks new hormone synthesis, but in thyroiditis the hormone is released from damaged follicles (hence low uptake), so antithyroid drugs do not help; carbimazole is right for Graves disease with diffuse high uptake.
key_concept:
Low uptake thyrotoxicosis = release, not synthesis: treat symptoms, not the gland.
  • Painful tender gland after viral illness: subacute thyroiditis
  • Treatment: beta blocker + NSAID; steroids if severe
  • Diffuse high uptake: Graves (antithyroid drugs)
  • Hyperthyroid phase may be followed by a hypothyroid phase
exam_pearl: High uptake would flip the answer to carbimazole; low uptake means beta blocker only.

stem:
A 72-Year-Old Man Presented With Acute Severe Chest Pain With An ECG Revealing ST Segment Elevation In II, III, AVF Leads And Was Treated With Thrombolysis. Two Days Later He Became Acutely Unwell With Severe Dyspnea. On Examination:
• Loud Systolic Murmur At The Apex Radiating To The Axilla
• Bilateral Crackles At The Base Of The Lungs
• Blood Pressure: 90/60 mmHg
• Heart Rate: 100 /min
• Respiratory Rate: 25 /min
• Oxygen Saturation: 88 %
Which Of The Following Is The Most Likely Diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: ST Segment Elevation In II, III, AVF
Loud Systolic Murmur At The Apex Radiating To The Axilla
why_right: Two days after an inferior STEMI (II, III, aVF) he develops sudden severe dyspnea with a new loud apical systolic murmur radiating to the axilla and bilateral basal crackles: this is acute mitral regurgitation causing pulmonary edema. Inferior MI particularly endangers the posteromedial papillary muscle, which has a single blood supply, so papillary muscle rupture is the most likely diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocarditis follows a viral illness in younger patients with diffuse ECG changes; it does not explain a new apical murmur 2 days after a thrombolysed STEMI.
B. Cardiogenic shock describes the haemodynamic state (BP 90/60) but not its cause; the murmur radiating to the axilla identifies the specific mechanical cause, which is what 'diagnosis' asks for.
D. Right sided failure (e.g. RV infarction) gives raised JVP, clear lungs and hypotension; here the lungs have crackles and the murmur is mitral, so the failure is left sided.
key_concept:
New murmur days after MI = mechanical complication; locate it by the murmur.
  • Apical pansystolic to axilla + pulmonary edema: papillary muscle rupture (acute MR)
  • Harsh left sternal border murmur + thrill + step up in O2 sat: VSD rupture
  • No murmur, sudden tamponade/PEA: free wall rupture
  • Inferior MI: posteromedial papillary muscle at risk
exam_pearl: Murmur at the left sternal border with a thrill flips the answer to ventricular septal rupture.

stem: Collage student asymptomatic denies chest pain or dyspnea or orthopnea found to have cardiomegaly on chest x ray and echocardiography showed left ventricular hypertrophy and ejection fraction of 40% What is the next management?
why_right: An asymptomatic young patient with cardiomegaly and EF 40% has reduced LV systolic function. ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril are the first step in reduced EF management and are indicated even without symptoms, because they slow remodeling and reduce progression to symptomatic heart failure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Repeating echo in 6 months leaves proven LV dysfunction untreated; watchful follow-up suits asymptomatic valve disease with preserved LV function, not EF 40%.
B. Digoxin only relieves symptoms or controls AF rate in established HFrEF and has no mortality benefit; it is not a first drug in an asymptomatic patient.
D. Furosemide treats congestion (edema, orthopnea, crackles); he denies dyspnea and orthopnea, so there is nothing to diurese.
key_concept:
Reduced EF, even asymptomatic: start ACE inhibitor (then add beta blocker).
  • Step 1: ACEi (ARB if cough)
  • Add: beta blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor
  • Diuretics: only for congestion
  • Digoxin: symptom control, no survival benefit
exam_pearl: Loop diuretics are for symptoms; ACEi is for the ejection fraction.

stem: Old patient known HTN on hydochlorothizide poorly controlled. Bp 153/102 Temp and heart rate (79) normal What diet modifications is needed for better control of his blood pressure?
why_right: An older patient with poorly controlled hypertension (153/102) on a thiazide needs dietary sodium restriction, the single diet change with the strongest blood pressure lowering effect. Older patients are particularly salt sensitive, and lowering salt intake also enhances the effect of the thiazide.
why_wrong_block:
A. A low fat diet helps lipids and weight and is part of DASH, but it is not the specific change that lowers blood pressure most.
C. Low protein diet is used to slow progression in advanced CKD, not to control essential hypertension.
D. High fiber is healthy and part of DASH, but its blood pressure effect is small compared with salt restriction; it is right for constipation or glycemic and lipid control.
key_concept:
For blood pressure, the most effective single dietary change is salt restriction.
  • Low sodium intake
  • DASH diet: fruits, vegetables, low fat dairy
  • Weight loss, exercise, limit alcohol
  • Low protein: reserved for CKD
exam_pearl: If the stem asks about CKD progression rather than blood pressure, low protein becomes the answer.

stem: Old patient 60 years k/c of hypertension and something else I forgot. on lisinopril and amlodipine and warfarin presented with productive cough and has positive AFB and was started on all 4 medication of TB (written like this). What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: started on all 4 medication of TB
why_right: The four drug TB regimen includes rifampicin, a potent liver enzyme inducer that speeds warfarin metabolism and lowers its effect. A patient on warfarin starting this regimen will become under anticoagulated, so the warfarin dose must be increased with close INR monitoring.
why_wrong_block:
A. Rifampicin is a core drug for active smear positive TB; the interaction is managed by adjusting warfarin, not by weakening the TB regimen. Stopping rifampicin is reserved for serious toxicity.
B. Lisinopril has no significant interaction with the anti-TB drugs that requires dose reduction.
C. Rifampicin can lower amlodipine levels, so if anything amlodipine may need more, not discontinuation; the clinically dangerous interaction here is with warfarin.
key_concept:
Rifampicin induces liver enzymes: drugs it lowers need higher doses.
  • Warfarin: increase dose, monitor INR closely
  • Oral contraceptives: become ineffective, use other contraception
  • Rifampicin: orange-red body fluids
  • Isoniazid: neuropathy, give pyridoxine
exam_pearl: When rifampicin is later stopped, warfarin must be reduced again or the INR overshoots.

stem: Patient with symptoms of Celiac disease. Has positive anti endomysial and anti TTG. Biopsy showed villous atrophy. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptA: Give gluten and retest for antibodies
highlight_terms_source: positive anti endomysial and anti TTG
why_right: Positive anti-endomysial and anti-tTG antibodies plus villous atrophy on biopsy confirm celiac disease, so the diagnosis is complete. The next step is treatment: strict lifelong gluten elimination (avoid wheat, barley and rye).
why_wrong_block:
A. A gluten challenge is used only when someone already stopped gluten before testing, making serology and biopsy unreliable; here the diagnosis is already confirmed.
B. Repeat biopsy is done when symptoms persist despite a strict gluten free diet (refractory disease or poor compliance), not right after a confirmed diagnosis.
key_concept:
Celiac workup: serology first, biopsy confirms, then lifelong gluten free diet.
  • First test: IgA tTG or anti-endomysial antibodies
  • Confirm: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Compliance follow-up: tTG levels fall on a strict diet
  • Association: dermatitis herpetiformis
exam_pearl: Persistent symptoms on diet: check compliance with tTG first, before repeat biopsy.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic for a check-up. She believes that she is allergic to wheat; her symptoms of abdominal bloating and loose stool have improved over the past few months by eating a gluten-free diet. Which of the following is the most appropriate advice to her?
OptC: No need to Continue on gluten-free diet
OptD: Resume eating gluten, bloods for celiac screen
why_right: Her bloating and loose stool settled on a self-started gluten-free diet, which raises suspicion of celiac disease rather than true wheat allergy. Celiac serology (IgA tTG) and duodenal biopsy only turn positive while gluten is being eaten, so testing her now risks a false negative. The most appropriate advice is to reintroduce gluten and then send celiac bloods.
why_wrong_block:
A. Dietitian input is valuable once celiac disease is confirmed and a lifelong diet is needed; referring now just entrenches an unproven diet and masks the diagnosis.
B. Specialist referral is for positive serology (to arrange biopsy) or alarm features; the first step of reintroducing gluten and screening can be done in primary care.
C. Simply stopping the diet without arranging serology wastes the chance to confirm or exclude celiac disease, which matters for long-term complications and family screening.
key_concept:
Celiac work-up is only valid on a gluten-containing diet.
  • Step 1: IgA tTG serology
  • Step 2: duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, intraepithelial lymphocytes)
  • Anti-endomysial antibody: second-line confirmatory serology
  • Treatment: lifelong gluten-free diet
  • tTG falling on diet = adherence monitoring
exam_pearl: Patient already gluten-free with suspected celiac: reintroduce gluten before any test, or serology and biopsy may be falsely normal.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Number printed at bottom of p542; the question is a screenshot at top of p543 with **D marked.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the clinic with symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease that not responding well to esomeprazole 20 mg once a day. Despite mild improvement in his symptoms, he continues to wake up with an acid taste in the middle of the night. He has not had difficulty swallowing. He confirms that he takes the medication properly. Physical examination is unremarkable. His laboratory investigation are within normal range. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
highlight_terms_source: acid taste in the middle of the night
why_right: He is on esomeprazole 20 mg once daily, which is below the usual full treatment dose, and has only partial relief with nocturnal acid taste. He is adherent, has no dysphagia and normal labs, so there are no alarm features. The next step is to optimise acid suppression by increasing the PPI dose before any investigation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Swapping one PPI for another at an equivalent low dose adds little; the problem is an inadequate dose, not the specific drug.
B. Endoscopy is for alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia) or GERD that stays refractory after an optimised PPI course; neither applies yet.
C. Amoxicillin plus clarithromycin is part of H. pylori eradication (with a PPI), which is indicated only after a positive H. pylori test, not for reflux symptoms.
key_concept:
Partial GERD response on PPI: optimise before investigating.
  • Check adherence and timing (before meals)
  • Low dose: increase to full dose; still poor: twice daily
  • Alarm features at any point: endoscopy
  • Refractory despite optimised PPI: endoscopy, then 24-hour pH monitoring if normal
  • Esophagitis with normal manometry and failed medical therapy: fundoplication
exam_pearl: Low-dose PPI with partial response and no alarm features = increase the dose; endoscopy only if alarm signs or failure at full dose.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version options: A. Increase esomeprazole dose, B. Add pantoprazole, C. Add clarithromycin and metronidazole. Screenshot marks **D.

stem: A 40-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with vomiting and generalized abdominal pain. She does not know her medications. She states that her vision has been slightly yellow tinged recently (see image). Blood pressure 90/50 mmHg, Heart rate 60 /min, Respiratory rate 16 /min, Temperature 37° C. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Yellow-tinged vision (xanthopsia) with vomiting and abdominal pain in a patient who does not know her medications is the classic picture of digoxin toxicity; GI upset is its most common symptom. The relatively slow heart rate of 60 with hypotension fits digoxin slowing AV conduction. The ECG in the recall shows the scooped (reverse tick) ST depression of digoxin effect, which confirms digoxin use.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anterolateral MI would show ST elevation in I, aVL and V5 to V6, not scooped ST depression, and it does not cause yellow vision.
C. Hypokalaemia is the commonest precipitant of digoxin toxicity and causes U waves and flat T waves, but on its own it does not produce xanthopsia.
D. Hypothermia gives bradycardia and J (Osborn) waves, but her temperature is a normal 37 C and it would not explain yellow vision.
key_concept:
Yellow vision + GI upset (+ arrhythmia) = digoxin toxicity.
  • Symptoms: nausea and vomiting (commonest), blurred or yellow vision, confusion
  • Arrhythmias: AV block, ectopics, atrial tachycardia with block
  • Precipitants: hypokalaemia, renal impairment, interacting drugs
  • Digoxin effect ECG: scooped reverse tick ST depression
  • Digoxin effect alone shows use, not toxicity
exam_pearl: Reverse tick ST depression means the patient is on digoxin; toxicity is diagnosed by symptoms and arrhythmia, not by that ST shape.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: Picture ECG (QRS-ST hockey stick) and yellow tinged vision; cause? A. Digoxin toxicity. ECG image not reproduced on this page.

stem: A 45-year old with chronic hepatitis B is noted to develop increasing jaundice for the last 2 weeks associated with fatigue (see lab results). Direct bilirubin 28.43 (1.5-6.5 umol/L); Total bilirubin 39 (3.5-16.5); AST 345 (12-40 IU/L); ALT 523 (5-40 IU/L); Albumin 34 (34-56 g/L); Total Proteins 60 (60-84); Hepatitis B DNA level Low. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: A known chronic hepatitis B patient suddenly develops an acute hepatitic picture over 2 weeks (AST 345, ALT 523, rising bilirubin) while HBV DNA is low. A flare driven by HBV itself would come with high viral replication, so low DNA points to a new insult, classically hepatitis D superinfection, which needs HBsAg to replicate. The next step is to request anti-delta antibody.
why_wrong_block:
A. Vitamin E is used in non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, a slow process; it has no role in an acute hepatitic flare with jaundice.
B. Liver biopsy is for staging fibrosis or unclear chronic disease; a non-invasive serology test should first identify the cause of this acute flare.
C. Interferon alpha is a treatment option for chronic HBV or HDV, but you must first establish the diagnosis; starting it blindly in an acutely jaundiced patient is inappropriate.
key_concept:
Chronic HBV + acute hepatitis + LOW HBV DNA = think hepatitis D superinfection.
  • HDV needs HBsAg to replicate (coinfection or superinfection)
  • Superinfection causes severe flares and faster progression to cirrhosis
  • Test: anti-HDV antibody (then HDV RNA)
  • High HBV DNA flare: HBV reactivation, treat with antivirals
  • Treated chronic HBV with raised enzymes: e.g. entecavir
exam_pearl: High HBV DNA flare = HBV reactivation; low HBV DNA flare = look for another virus, especially delta.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall version: chronic HBV now jaundiced, elevated enzymes and bilirubin, HBV DNA -ve; options A. Interferon alpha, B. Liver biopsy, C. CT abdomen, D. Delta antigen test. Screenshot marks **D.

stem: Patient presents to clinic complaining of recurrent chest pain. He has chest pain with heavy exercise but relieved with rest. Resting ECG normal and he has no past medical history or comorbidities. What next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: chest pain with heavy exercise but relieved with rest
why_right: Chest pain with heavy exercise, relieved by rest is typical of stable angina. With a normal resting ECG and a patient who can clearly exercise, the next step is an exercise (stress) ECG to look for inducible ischaemia. A positive test then leads to coronary angiography.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myocardial perfusion (nuclear) imaging is chosen when the resting ECG is abnormal (LBBB, paced rhythm, ST changes) or the patient cannot exercise, using pharmacological stress.
B. A resting echo assesses structure and function (valves, wall motion, LV function) but cannot detect exercise-induced ischaemia; stress echo is used if the resting ECG is abnormal.
D. Coronary angiography is invasive and reserved for a positive stress test, high-risk features or acute coronary syndrome, not as the first test in stable exertional pain.
key_concept:
Stable exertional chest pain work-up depends on the resting ECG and ability to exercise.
  • Normal resting ECG + can exercise: exercise ECG
  • Abnormal resting ECG: stress echo or nuclear perfusion
  • Cannot exercise: pharmacological stress (dobutamine echo, adenosine or dipyridamole perfusion)
  • Positive stress test: coronary angiography
  • 1 to 2 vessel disease: PCI; 3 vessel or left main: CABG
exam_pearl: If the stem gives LBBB or another abnormal baseline ECG, the answer flips from exercise ECG to stress imaging.

stem: Patient came with typical chest pain and sweating. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with LBBB. Previous ECG is normal. Started on aspirin, atorvastatin, Nitroglycerin, Beta blocker and morphine. Cardiac enzyme is pending. What is the next step?
why_right: Typical chest pain with sweating plus LBBB with a previously normal ECG (new LBBB) is managed as a STEMI equivalent. Reperfusion must not be delayed for troponin, and urgent coronary angiography with primary PCI is the preferred reperfusion strategy when available; thrombolysis is the alternative when PCI cannot be done in time.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV lidocaine treats sustained ventricular arrhythmias; there is no ventricular tachycardia here and prophylactic lidocaine in MI is not recommended.
B. Waiting for enzymes delays reperfusion; with ischaemic symptoms and new LBBB the decision is made on the clinical picture and ECG.
D. Discharge is dangerous: this is a presumed acute MI needing emergency reperfusion and admission.
key_concept:
Ischaemic chest pain + new (or presumed new) LBBB = treat as STEMI.
  • Do not wait for troponin
  • Preferred: urgent angiography with primary PCI
  • PCI not available in time: thrombolysis
  • Adjuncts: aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation, nitrates if BP allows
  • Known old LBBB: use Sgarbossa criteria to judge acute MI
exam_pearl: If the option list has thrombolysis but not angiography, thrombolysis is the reperfusion answer; both mean the same decision: reperfuse now.

stem: 78 years old known case of DM2 HTN and CKD admitted to hospital due to confusion and fluctuant of consciousness taking multiple drugs (written like this) his temperature is Fever 39 C. Urine analysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, WBC 50, protein negative, glucose +1. Which of the following is the best next step?
OptD: Order blood and urine culture and start Antibiotics
why_right: An elderly diabetic with CKD has acute fluctuating confusion (delirium) with fever 39 C and urine showing positive leukocyte esterase and pyuria (WBC 50). This is a febrile, complicated UTI (possible urosepsis) as the likely cause of delirium. The best next step is to send blood and urine cultures and start empirical IV antibiotics without delay.
why_wrong_block:
A. Head CT is for focal neurological signs, head trauma or anticoagulation; here a clear infective source already explains the delirium.
B. Polypharmacy is a common cause of delirium and should be reviewed, but with high fever and pyuria, untreated infection is the urgent priority.
C. Lumbar puncture is for suspected meningitis (neck stiffness, headache, photophobia) or when no other source of fever and confusion is found; the urine already shows a source.
key_concept:
Elderly + fever + delirium + abnormal urine = treat as complicated UTI or urosepsis.
  • Cultures (blood and urine) before antibiotics, but do not delay antibiotics
  • Diabetes, CKD and older age make the UTI complicated
  • Delirium work-up: infection, drugs, metabolic, hypoxia, retention, constipation
  • Neuroimaging only if focal signs, trauma or no cause found
exam_pearl: Afebrile elderly with confusion and an incidental positive dipstick is a trap (asymptomatic bacteriuria); here the 39 C fever makes infection the answer.

stem: Elderly women with recurrent UTIs (didn’t mention number of times per year). Best clinical proven way to prevent recurrent UTIs?
why_right: This recall keys increased fluid intake as the clinically proven measure because a randomised trial showed that drinking extra water reduced recurrent cystitis in women with low baseline fluid intake. More fluid increases urine flow and bladder emptying, flushing bacteria before they can establish infection. It is simple, safe and suits an elderly woman.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cranberry products have mixed evidence across trials and are often taken as a supplement; this recall does not treat them as the best-proven measure.
C. Avoiding tight clothing is common lay advice with no good evidence of reducing UTI recurrence.
D. Voiding after intercourse is a behavioural tip for young sexually active women with postcoital UTIs, but its evidence is weak and less relevant to an elderly woman; proven postcoital prevention is a single-dose antibiotic.
key_concept:
Recurrent UTI prevention ladder.
  • Behavioural: increase fluid intake (best supported simple measure)
  • Postmenopausal women: vaginal estrogen
  • Intercourse-related: postcoital single-dose antibiotic
  • Frequent recurrences despite measures: continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis
  • Adjuncts with mixed evidence: cranberry, methenamine
exam_pearl: If the stem says UTIs follow intercourse, the answer shifts to postcoital single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Other versions in block: (1) 12yo with recent UTI, mother asks how to prevent: A/ Hygiene after intercourse, B/ drink sugary drinks, C/ use something, D/ keep hygiene and clean; 'No Hydration' in that recall. (2) 40yo healthy female, recurrent UTI 4 times in 1 year, best evidence-based prevention: A-Hydration, B-Cranberry juice, C-Postcoital hygiene, D-Prophylactic abx; Answer: A.

stem: Female RA around 35 years patient on Methotrexate, ask dr about vaccination as she afraid from influenza and pneumonia
OptA: give live influenza vaccine and No pneumococcal
OptB: give inactivated influenza vaccine and pneumococcal conjugated
OptC: don't give any as she is immunocompromised
OptD: let her stop methotrexate and return to take vaccine
why_right: Methotrexate makes her immunosuppressed, so live vaccines should be avoided, but inactivated vaccines are safe and strongly recommended because her infection risk is higher. She fears influenza and pneumonia, so she should receive the inactivated (injectable) influenza vaccine yearly and pneumococcal conjugate vaccination, without stopping methotrexate.
why_wrong_block:
A. The live attenuated (intranasal) influenza vaccine is contraindicated on immunosuppressants, and withholding pneumococcal vaccine leaves her unprotected against pneumonia.
C. Immunosuppression is a reason to give inactivated vaccines, not to withhold them; only live vaccines are avoided.
D. Stopping methotrexate risks an RA flare and is unnecessary for inactivated vaccines; it may be paused briefly only in specific situations, not stopped as a precondition.
key_concept:
Immunosuppressed adult: give all inactivated vaccines, avoid live ones.
  • Inactivated or non-live: injectable influenza, pneumococcal conjugate (plus PPSV23 if the conjugate used requires it), hepatitis A and B, tetanus, HPV, recombinant zoster
  • Live (avoid): intranasal influenza, MMR, varicella, live zoster, yellow fever, BCG, oral typhoid
  • Ideally vaccinate before starting immunosuppression
  • Methotrexate does not need to be stopped for inactivated vaccines
exam_pearl: Immunocompromised does not mean no vaccines; it means no live vaccines.

stem: Patient complains of heart burn on pantoprazole (dose was not mentioned), he is not improving, what the next step in management?
why_right: This recall's key is testing for H. pylori because in a patient whose upper GI acid symptoms do not improve on pantoprazole, an untreated H. pylori infection (gastritis or peptic ulcer) can mimic reflux and will not settle on acid suppression alone. Test-and-treat is non-invasive and, if positive, eradication addresses the cause.
why_wrong_block:
A. Upper endoscopy is the step for alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia, older age) or reflux refractory to an optimised PPI; the stem gives none of these.
B. Increasing the PPI dose is the usual step for true GERD on a low or partial dose; the recall instead keys finding a treatable cause first.
key_concept:
Poor response to PPI: confirm adherence, then optimise or investigate.
  • Dyspepsia without alarm features: H. pylori test and treat
  • Typical GERD on low-dose PPI: increase dose, then twice daily
  • Alarm features or failure of optimised PPI: endoscopy
  • Normal endoscopy: 24-hour pH monitoring
  • Stop PPI 2 weeks before urea breath or stool antigen test (false negatives)
exam_pearl: Heartburn with a stated low dose and partial response (as in the esomeprazole 20 mg card) is keyed to increasing the dose, not H. pylori.

stem: Women on OCPs came complaining of chest pain for 4 or 5 hours. Trop was less than the normal range mentioned in exam. What is the initial management?
highlight_terms_source: Trop was less than the normal range
why_right: A woman on OCPs (an estrogen VTE risk factor) with hours of chest pain and a normal troponin points away from ACS and toward pulmonary embolism. Nothing in the stem suggests shock, so this is a hemodynamically stable suspected PE, and the initial management is anticoagulation (LMWH or heparin), started even while imaging is arranged when suspicion is high.
why_wrong_block:
B. Thrombolysis is reserved for PE with unstable circulation (hypotension, shock); a stable patient gains little and carries a major bleeding risk.
C. An IVC filter is used only when anticoagulation is contraindicated or PE recurs despite adequate anticoagulation; neither applies here.
key_concept:
Suspected or confirmed PE: assess circulation first, then choose the treatment.
  • Stable circulation: LMWH or heparin, then oral anticoagulant
  • Unstable (massive PE): thrombolysis
  • Unstable and thrombolysis contraindicated or failed: embolectomy
  • Anticoagulation contraindicated or recurrent PE on it: IVC filter
  • Warfarin is long term, never the acute first step
exam_pearl: Chest pain with a normal troponin in an OCP user is PE until proven otherwise; only hypotension switches the answer to thrombolysis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer printed as 'A?' (compiler uncertain).

stem: Pt take fentanyl drug as analgesia for joint pain came c/o decrease level of consciousness and tremor, LFT increase 3fold (I think known CKD), cause?
highlight_terms_source: decrease level of consciousness and tremor
key_concept:
Approach to new confusion: look for the trigger the stem emphasises.
  • Alcohol or malnutrition + eye signs + ataxia: Wernicke
  • High urea, asterixis, pericardial rub: uremic encephalopathy, dialysis
  • New or increased drug, especially with renal or hepatic impairment: drug toxicity
  • Opioid toxicity: miosis, respiratory depression, reversed by naloxone
  • Serotonin toxicity: tremor, clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia
exam_pearl: Let the stem's dominant clue decide: a quoted high urea points to uremia, alcohol or malnutrition with eye signs points to Wernicke, and a new or escalated drug with reduced clearance points to drug toxicity.

stem: COPD pt complain of SOB and cough for 3 months, pH 7.25 I can’t remember the number sorry. Ask about dx?
OptA: COPD due to mix resp failure
OptB: COPD due to acute resp failure type 1
OptC: COPD due to acute resp failure type 2
OptD: COPD due to chronic resp failure
key_concept:
Read the ABG in three steps: PaO2, PaCO2, then pH and HCO3.
  • Type 1: low PaO2, normal or low PaCO2
  • Type 2: low PaO2, high PaCO2
  • Acute type 2: high PaCO2, low pH, HCO3 normal
  • Chronic type 2: high PaCO2, near-normal pH, high HCO3
  • Acute on chronic: high PaCO2, high HCO3, but pH still low
  • Mixed: high PaCO2 with low HCO3
exam_pearl: The pH decides acute versus chronic: a COPD patient with high CO2 but near-normal pH is chronic; a low pH means acute decompensation.

stem: 35-year-old male presents with dizziness and fatigue that worsen after meals. On examination, he is pale and jaundiced. He does not take any medication except omeprazole. Laboratory tests show anemia and increased bilirubin (mainly direct/dark). What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A young male with episodic fatigue and dizziness that worsen after meals, plus pallor, jaundice and dark urine, describes episodic hemolysis triggered by an oxidant food, classically fava beans. G6PD deficiency is X-linked (so seen in males) and causes intermittent hemolytic crises after oxidant foods, drugs or infection. His only drug, omeprazole, is not a recognised oxidant trigger.
why_wrong_block:
A. Cold agglutinin disease is IgM mediated and triggered by cold exposure (acrocyanosis), often after Mycoplasma or EBV or with lymphoproliferative disease, not by meals.
B. Warm AIHA is diagnosed by a positive Coombs test, often with spherocytes and an autoimmune or lymphoproliferative background; nothing here links episodes to food.
C. Drug-induced hemolysis needs an oxidant or immune trigger drug (sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, primaquine, dapsone, high-dose aspirin); omeprazole is not one, and the meal timing fits a food trigger.
key_concept:
Hemolysis plus a clear trigger points to the cause.
  • Fava beans, mothballs, oxidant drugs, infection: G6PD deficiency (Heinz bodies, bite cells)
  • Cold exposure: cold agglutinin (IgM, C3 only Coombs)
  • Coombs IgG positive, spherocytes: warm AIHA, steroids first line
  • Triggering drugs: primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin, quinolones, high-dose aspirin
exam_pearl: Hemolysis raises unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin with dark urine from hemoglobin; do not let a recalled 'direct bilirubin' steer you to liver disease when the trigger is food.

stem: A 60-something-year-old man with known COPD, controlled with bronchodilators, comes for a routine follow-up. He quit smoking 12 years ago. His oxygen saturation ranges from 89% to 91%. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This is a routine follow-up of controlled COPD in an ex-smoker, so the task is preventive care. Vaccination (pneumococcal, plus annual influenza) reduces infections and exacerbations and is one of the interventions that improve outcome in COPD. His SpO2 of 89 to 91% without complications does not meet home oxygen criteria.
why_wrong_block:
A. Long-term azithromycin is added for frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy; this patient is controlled with no exacerbations described.
C. Home oxygen needs SpO2 below 88% (or PaO2 below 55 mmHg) on two readings, or 88 to 92% plus edema, pulmonary hypertension, nocturnal hypoxia or polycythemia; none is present here.
key_concept:
COPD outcome-improving measures: smoking cessation, long-term oxygen when criteria are met, vaccination.
  • SpO2 <88% or PaO2 <55 mmHg on 2 readings: home oxygen
  • SpO2 88 to 92% plus edema, pulmonary HTN, nocturnal hypoxia or high hematocrit: home oxygen
  • Otherwise SpO2 88 to 92% is an acceptable COPD target
  • Stable visit: inhaler review, vaccines, rehab
exam_pearl: An SpO2 just under 92% tempts you to give oxygen; without cor pulmonale, edema or polycythemia it does not qualify.

stem: Positive comb test + normal kidney function (mentioned in labs urea & creat)?
key_concept:
Hemolysis + low platelets: first ask Coombs, then the kidneys.
  • Coombs positive + low platelets: Evans syndrome (AIHA + ITP)
  • Coombs negative + schistocytes + AKI: HUS
  • Coombs negative + schistocytes + fever, neuro signs: TTP
  • Abnormal PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer: DIC
exam_pearl: TTP and HUS are mechanical (Coombs negative); a positive Coombs test points to an autoimmune process such as Evans syndrome.

stem: Endoscopy: urease negative for pt complaining of epigastric pain?
OptB: Another test for h. Pylori (don't remember)
key_concept:
H. pylori tests: invasive (needs endoscopy) versus non-invasive.
  • Invasive: rapid urease test, histology, culture (culture for resistance after failures)
  • Non-invasive: urea breath test, stool antigen
  • Test of cure: urea breath test or stool antigen, never serology
  • False negatives: PPI within 2 weeks, antibiotics or bismuth within 4 weeks
exam_pearl: A negative test on PPI is not reassuring; repeat with a different method after a washout rather than accepting it.

stem: Old age HTN non compliant to medications, come with rt side weakness , slurred speech , examination agitated, rt or lt pupil dilated > other 1mm , Bp 160/90 ,Ct brain free ?
key_concept:
Stroke imaging ladder:
  • First: non-contrast CT to exclude hemorrhage before any thrombolysis or antithrombotic
  • CT normal but stroke suspected: MRI with DWI to confirm infarct
  • Vessel imaging (CTA, MRA, carotid duplex): find large-artery occlusion or stenosis
  • Cardiac work-up (ECG monitoring, echo) for embolic source
exam_pearl: A normal early CT does not exclude ischemic stroke; it only excludes bleeding. A 1 mm pupil difference is often physiological anisocoria.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who delivered 5 months ago presents with fatigue, dizziness, and failure to breastfeed her baby. Her obstetrical history reveals a vaginal delivery complicated by a retained placenta and severe postpartum hemorrhage. On evaluation, her free T4 level is low (4 mmol/L). What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Failure to breastfeed, fatigue and dizziness months after retained placenta with severe PPH is Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis). With a low free T4, the next step is to order TSH: a low or inappropriately normal TSH confirms central (secondary) hypothyroidism rather than primary thyroid failure, before any hormone is replaced.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thyroxine should not be started before the diagnosis is confirmed, and in pituitary failure giving thyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement can precipitate adrenal crisis.
C. Estrogen replacement is part of later long-term management of hypopituitarism, not the next step, and it does not address the thyroid or adrenal deficit.
D. No sodium level or severe neurological symptoms are given; hypertonic saline is only for severe symptomatic hyponatremia.
key_concept:
Sheehan syndrome: PPH leads to pituitary infarction and hypopituitarism.
  • Earliest sign: failure of lactation (low prolactin)
  • Then amenorrhea, fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia
  • Low free T4 + low or normal TSH = central hypothyroidism
  • Check cortisol (ACTH axis) too
  • Replace steroids before thyroxine
exam_pearl: In suspected pituitary failure, never give thyroxine first: steroids before thyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis.

stem: A patient who is a known case of Crohn's disease presents with bouts of bloody diarrhea and left-sided abdominal pain. The patient is currently taking prednisone 50 mg daily. A sigmoidoscopy is performed and reveals recurrent patchy colitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: This patient with known Crohn's disease is flaring ("recurrent patchy colitis", bloody diarrhea) while already on prednisone 50 mg daily. Relapse on a full steroid dose means steroid-refractory or steroid-dependent disease, so steroids have failed and therapy must be escalated. An anti-TNF agent (infliximab or adalimumab) is the step used for refractory Crohn's disease to induce and then maintain remission.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ileal-release steroids (budesonide) are a first-line induction option for mild to moderate ileocecal Crohn's; this patient is already failing a high-dose systemic steroid, and an ileal-release drug would not target colonic disease anyway.
C. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are for septic complications such as a perianal abscess or fistula infection; nothing here suggests an abscess, and antibiotics do not control an inflammatory flare.
D. Mesalamine is the mainstay for mild to moderate ulcerative colitis but has little benefit in Crohn's disease, and it would be a step down for someone flaring on steroids.
key_concept:
Crohn's flare despite steroids = escalate to biologic therapy.
  • Induction: steroids (ileal-release budesonide for ileocecal disease, systemic or IV steroids for more severe disease)
  • Maintenance: immunomodulators (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine)
  • Refractory, steroid-dependent or fistulizing disease: anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab)
  • Steroids induce remission; they are never maintenance
  • Mesalamine: UC drug, minimal role in Crohn's
exam_pearl: "Already on prednisone" plus a new flare means steroid failure, so the answer is a biologic, not another steroid.

stem: A 72-year-old man is brought to the clinic by his wife due to episodes where he suddenly stops speaking, develops a blank, staring look, and displays repetitive facial grimacing and lip-smacking. Each episode lasts for 1 to 2 minutes, after which he is temporarily confused. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Episodes in which he suddenly stops talking with a blank stare, lip-smacking and facial grimacing (oral automatisms) lasting 1 to 2 minutes, followed by temporary confusion, describe a focal seizure with impaired awareness. Oral automatisms are the hallmark of a temporal lobe origin, and postictal confusion confirms a seizure rather than a vascular event. New-onset focal seizures in an older adult are common and need imaging to look for a structural cause such as prior stroke or a tumor.
why_wrong_block:
B. Typical absence seizures occur in children (classically 5 to 8 years), last only seconds, and end abruptly with no postictal confusion; this is a 72-year-old with 1 to 2 minute episodes and confusion afterward.
C. A TIA causes negative focal deficits (weakness, numbness, speech or vision loss) without automatisms like lip-smacking, and it is not followed by postictal confusion.
D. Frontotemporal dementia causes a gradual, persistent change in behavior or language, usually starting before 65; it does not cause brief stereotyped episodes with recovery in between.
key_concept:
Blank stare + automatisms + postictal confusion = focal impaired-awareness (temporal lobe) seizure.
  • Temporal lobe: lip-smacking, chewing, hand fumbling, 1 to 2 minutes, postictal confusion
  • Absence: child, seconds, no postictal state, 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG
  • TIA: sudden negative deficit, no automatisms
  • FTD: progressive personality or language change, no episodes
exam_pearl: Postictal confusion separates a focal seizure from an absence seizure, which ends abruptly and leaves the patient fully alert.

stem: A 40-year-old man medically and surgically free is evaluated in the Emergency Department for several episodes of hematemesis. He has no previous similar episodes and takes no medications. There is no jaundice, splenomegaly, or other signs of chronic liver disease. Abdominal examination reveals no tenderness, guarding, or rebound. Lab results: BP: 105/65 mmHg, HR: 110/min, Temp: 36.8°C, Hb: 95 g/L (low), Platelets: 250 × 10⁹/L, WBC: 12 × 10⁹/L, LFTs: normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his gastrointestinal bleeding?
highlight_terms_source: no jaundice, splenomegaly, or other signs of chronic liver disease
why_right: A previously healthy 40-year-old with first-time hematemesis and no medications, and no jaundice, splenomegaly or chronic liver stigmata, with normal LFTs and a normal platelet count, has no pointer to portal hypertension or a specific precipitant. Peptic ulcer disease is the most common cause of upper GI bleeding, so it is the most likely source. The tachycardia (HR 110) and Hb of 95 g/L show a significant bleed that needs resuscitation and early endoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Erosive gastritis is the typical cause in heavy alcohol users, NSAID users or critically ill (stress) patients; the stem gives none of these (he takes no medications), and gastritis usually causes minor oozing rather than a bleed with tachycardia.
C. Esophageal varices need portal hypertension; there are no signs of chronic liver disease, no splenomegaly, and LFTs and platelets are normal.
D. A Mallory-Weiss tear presents with hematemesis that follows repeated or forceful vomiting; the stem gives no history of preceding vomiting.
key_concept:
Upper GI bleed: let the background choose the cause.
  • No risk factors, normal liver = peptic ulcer disease (most common)
  • Stigmata of chronic liver disease, low platelets = varices
  • Bleeding after forceful vomiting = Mallory-Weiss tear
  • Alcohol, NSAIDs or critical illness = erosive gastritis
exam_pearl: If the stem carefully lists "no jaundice, no splenomegaly, normal LFTs", it is ruling out varices, so choose PUD.

stem: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus presents to the Emergency Department with a 2-day history of generalized tonic-clonic seizures and severe fatigue. Musculoskeletal and neurological examinations are otherwise normal. She is initiated on intravenous methylprednisolone. Brain MRI reveals multiple hyperintense lesions. Which of the following medications is the most appropriate additional treatment to control her disease flares?
why_right: A young woman with SLE who develops generalized seizures with multiple hyperintense lesions on brain MRI has neuropsychiatric lupus, a severe, organ-threatening flare. IV methylprednisolone has been started, and the recommended additional immunosuppressant for severe neuropsychiatric (and renal) lupus is cyclophosphamide. The lead-in asks what controls the disease flare, not the seizure itself.
why_wrong_block:
B. Azathioprine is a steroid-sparing maintenance agent with a slow onset; it fits mild to moderate disease or maintenance after induction, not induction for severe neuropsychiatric lupus.
C. Phenytoin may control the seizures symptomatically, but it does not treat the underlying lupus flare, which is what the question asks about.
D. Heparin would be the choice if the brain lesions were thrombotic from antiphospholipid syndrome; the stem gives no antiphospholipid antibodies, thrombosis or pregnancy loss, and asks for flare control.
key_concept:
Severe organ-threatening SLE (CNS or renal) = high-dose steroids + cyclophosphamide.
  • Mild SLE: hydroxychloroquine (± NSAID)
  • Moderate: add low-dose steroid, steroid-sparing agents (azathioprine)
  • Severe neuropsychiatric or renal lupus: IV methylprednisolone + cyclophosphamide (or mycophenolate for nephritis)
  • Seizures from APS-related thrombosis: anticoagulation
exam_pearl: "Additional treatment to control her disease" asks for immunosuppression, so an antiepileptic is a trap even though she is seizing.

stem: 30 yo man with one week hx of jaundice, RUQ pain and fatigue, no mention of any chronic illness or risk factors ALT 1000 AST 850 what type of ACUTE hepatitis infection this pt have? (the word Acute was written in the Stem)
highlight_terms_source: no mention of any chronic illness or risk factors
why_right: This recall's key is hepatitis B. A 30-year-old with one week of jaundice, RUQ pain and fatigue and transaminases near 1000 has acute viral hepatitis. Among the options, hepatitis C rarely causes symptomatic acute icteric hepatitis, and hepatitis D cannot infect without hepatitis B. Between A and B, the key relies on the patient being an adult: in endemic regions most adults acquired hepatitis A in childhood and are immune, while adults who acquire hepatitis B are often symptomatic and icteric.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hepatitis A is the classic cause of acute hepatitis with a short incubation and would be favored in a nonimmune patient or after a food or water exposure; this key assumes an adult who is already immune from childhood infection.
C. Acute hepatitis C is usually asymptomatic or mild and rarely presents with jaundice and transaminases near 1000; HCV is recognized mainly as chronic infection.
D. Hepatitis D is a defective virus that needs HBsAg; it presents as coinfection with HBV or as an acute flare in a known chronic HBV carrier, and neither is described here.
key_concept:
Acute hepatitis picture = ALT/AST in the hundreds to thousands with jaundice.
  • HAV: fecal-oral, short incubation, test anti-HAV IgM, never chronic
  • HBV: sexual or blood, weeks to months incubation, test HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM
  • HCV: blood-borne, acute phase usually silent, mostly chronic
  • HDV: only with HBV; acute flare in a chronic HBV carrier = check anti-HDV
exam_pearl: No stated exposure plus an adult patient is what this key leans on; if the stem mentioned travel, contaminated food or a child, hepatitis A would win.

stem: Patient with Epigastric pain improving with calcium carbonate. On exam tenderness in hypochondriac region FOBT positive Colonoscopy normal Next best step
highlight_terms_source: Epigastric pain improving with calcium carbonate
why_right: A positive FOBT with a normal colonoscopy means the occult blood is likely coming from the upper GI tract. Epigastric pain relieved by calcium carbonate (an antacid) points to an acid-related lesion such as a peptic ulcer, which can bleed slowly and give a positive FOBT. The next best step is esophagogastroduodenoscopy to find the source, take biopsies and test for H. pylori.
why_wrong_block:
B. Empiric omeprazole is acceptable for uncomplicated dyspepsia without alarm features; GI blood loss is an alarm feature, so the lesion must be seen (and malignancy excluded) before treating blindly.
C. Exploratory laparotomy is for an acute abdomen (peritonitis, perforation) or uncontrolled bleeding; this patient has only tenderness and occult blood loss.
D. This option was not recalled; it cannot be assessed, and EGD remains the next step for occult GI bleeding with a negative colonoscopy and upper GI symptoms.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT: colonoscopy first; if normal, look upstream.
  • Positive FOBT always needs investigation, starting with colonoscopy
  • Normal colonoscopy + dyspeptic symptoms = EGD
  • Normal colonoscopy + normal EGD = small bowel evaluation (capsule endoscopy)
  • GI bleeding is an alarm feature: scope, do not just give a PPI
exam_pearl: Pain eased by antacids is the clue that redirects a positive FOBT from the colon to the stomach and duodenum.

stem: A guy came from India, with meningitis symptoms ( headache neck rigidity photosensitivity) CSF shows - low glucose - slightly high protein - lymphocytosis what could be the causitive organism?
why_right: The CSF shows low glucose with lymphocytosis and raised protein, and the patient comes from India, a TB-endemic country. Low glucose excludes viral meningitis, and lymphocytes rather than neutrophils argue against bacterial meningitis. That combination is the classic profile of tuberculous meningitis, which typically has a subacute course and markedly raised protein.
why_wrong_block:
B. Viral meningitis gives lymphocytosis but a normal glucose and normal or mildly raised protein; the low glucose here excludes it.
C. Bacterial meningitis also lowers glucose but gives a neutrophil-predominant CSF, usually with turbid fluid and an acute course; this CSF is lymphocytic.
D. Fungal (cryptococcal) meningitis can give a similar CSF but occurs mainly in immunocompromised patients such as advanced HIV; no immunosuppression is mentioned, and the endemic origin favors TB.
key_concept:
CSF: glucose plus cell type picks the organism.
  • Bacterial: low glucose, high protein, neutrophils
  • Viral: normal glucose, normal or mildly high protein, lymphocytes
  • TB: low glucose, very high protein, lymphocytes, subacute, endemic origin
  • Fungal: low glucose, lymphocytes, immunocompromised (India ink or cryptococcal antigen)
exam_pearl: Low glucose plus lymphocytes is TB until proven otherwise; switch to fungal only if the stem says HIV or immunosuppression.

stem: Man came from holiday with chest XR showing signs of ARDS (literally written like that) + labs showing sodium 122 what’s the causative agent
why_right: Severe pneumonia that progresses to ARDS in a man returning from holiday (hotels, cruise ships, air-conditioning and water systems) with hyponatremia (Na 122) is the classic picture of Legionella pneumophila. Legionella is an atypical organism that causes severe pneumonia with extrapulmonary features such as hyponatremia, GI upset, confusion and deranged LFTs. Diagnosis is by urinary antigen, and treatment is a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone, because beta-lactams do not cover it.
why_wrong_block: B. The other options were not recalled. Likely alternatives: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common community pneumonia, no travel link or hyponatremia), Mycoplasma (young patients, mild walking pneumonia, cold agglutinins), and Staphylococcus aureus (after influenza, cavitating lesions).
key_concept:
Pneumonia + travel or hotel stay + hyponatremia = Legionella.
  • Source: contaminated water, air conditioning, cooling towers, hot tubs
  • Clues: hyponatremia, diarrhea, confusion, high fever, abnormal LFTs
  • Test: urinary antigen
  • Treat: macrolide (azithromycin) or fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin)
exam_pearl: Low sodium with pneumonia is the single strongest clue for Legionella; add travel or air conditioning and it is the answer.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is evaluated in follow-up after a 5 mm pulmonary nodule was discovered on chest imaging obtained 9 months ago. She feels well and has not had shortness of breath, cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or chest pain. She has a 50-pack-year smoking history and is a recurrent smoker. Examination revealed normal vital signs, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and clear lungs to auscultation bilaterally (see report). Repeated chest CT: Interval increase in the size of the nodule, now measuring 10.5 mm in diameter, and no evidence of mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptB: Repeat chest CT imaging in 6 months
highlight_terms_source: Interval increase in the size of the nodule, now measuring 10.5 mm
why_right: A nodule that grew from 5 mm to 10.5 mm in 9 months in a 50 pack-year, still-smoking 68-year-old is highly suspicious for lung cancer. Interval growth defeats any "watch and wait" plan, and with no nodal disease she should be referred to thoracic surgery for tissue diagnosis and likely resection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Lung biopsies should be image guided (CT-guided), never blind; a blind aspiration of a 1 cm nodule is unsafe and low yield.
B. Repeat CT in 6 months is for a stable, small, low-risk nodule; this one has already shown significant growth, so waiting delays a cancer diagnosis.
D. Bronchoscopy has low yield for small peripheral nodules; it is better for central lesions or endobronchial disease.
key_concept:
Solitary pulmonary nodule by size and behaviour:
  • 4 mm or less, low risk: no follow up
  • More than 4 to 8 mm: CT follow up at 3 to 6 months
  • More than 8 mm to 2 cm: PET/CT then image-guided biopsy
  • More than 2 cm: baseline PFT then surgery
  • Any interval growth: refer to thoracic surgery
  • Stable for 2 to 3 years: benign, stop follow up
exam_pearl: Growth beats size: a growing nodule in a heavy smoker goes to surgery even if it is only about 1 cm.

stem: A 50-year-old man is evaluated in the clinic for newly diagnosed hypertension that is not well controlled with lifestyle modifications. His systemic examinations are unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient's hypertension?
highlight_terms_source: not well controlled with lifestyle modifications
why_right: This recall's key is lisinopril plus amlodipine: hypertension that is "not well controlled with lifestyle modifications" in a patient with an unremarkable exam is keyed to initial dual therapy with an ACE inhibitor plus a calcium channel blocker. Starting two first line classes together is accepted when BP is well above target. The original question gives no BP values or labs, so learn this as the keyed answer for this exact stem.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amlodipine alone is a valid first line monotherapy for milder (stage 1) hypertension, but this key prefers the ACE inhibitor plus CCB combination.
B. Lisinopril alone would be first choice with diabetes and proteinuria or CKD; this stem has no such clue and is keyed to combination therapy.
C. A thiazide is also a first line class and would suit monotherapy for mild elevation, but it is not the keyed choice here.
key_concept:
First line classes: ACE inhibitor/ARB, CCB, thiazide.
  • Stage 1: lifestyle first, then one agent if not controlled
  • BP well above target (stage 2): start two agents, e.g. ACE inhibitor + CCB
  • Diabetes with proteinuria or CKD: ACE inhibitor/ARB
  • Avoid ACE inhibitor + ARB together
exam_pearl: If the stem gives diabetes with proteinuria, the single ACE inhibitor wins; without it, this recall is keyed to the combination.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0044 (lab results not shown in recall); screenshot and compiler both say D.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the clinic with decreased exercise tolerance and ice cravings for the past several months. Medical history is notable for celiac disease diagnosed 7 years ago, and she is not compliant with a gluten-free diet. Her only medication is ferrous sulfate tablets 325 mg once daily, which she has been taking for 12 weeks after being diagnosed with iron deficiency anemia. Examination reveals a thin patient with normal vital signs, pale conjunctivae, and nail beds. Cardiac examination reveals a grade 2/6 systolic flow murmur (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
OptC: Oral iron in a liquid preparation
OptD: Oral iron tablets three times daily
highlight_terms_source: not compliant with a gluten-free diet
why_right: She is still symptomatic ("ice cravings", "pale conjunctivae", "systolic flow murmur") after 12 weeks of daily ferrous sulfate, so oral iron has failed. The cause is obvious: celiac disease with poor adherence to a gluten free diet damages the duodenum and proximal jejunum, exactly where iron is absorbed. When oral iron fails because of malabsorption, IV iron bypasses the gut and is the most appropriate treatment (alongside strict gluten avoidance).
why_wrong_block:
A. Continuing the same tablets ignores a failed 12 week trial; she remains pale with pica and a flow murmur. Continuing is right only when Hb is rising appropriately on oral iron.
C. A liquid formulation still depends on duodenal absorption, which active celiac disease impairs. Liquid iron suits children or patients who cannot swallow tablets, not malabsorption.
D. More frequent oral doses do not overcome villous atrophy and add GI side effects; frequent dosing also raises hepcidin and can lower fractional absorption.
key_concept:
Oral iron failure + malabsorption = switch to IV iron.
  • First line IDA: oral ferrous sulfate
  • Adequate trial with persistent anemia: check adherence, ongoing loss, malabsorption
  • Malabsorption causes: celiac disease, bariatric surgery, atrophic gastritis, H. pylori
  • IV iron also for intolerance of oral iron or need for rapid repletion
  • Pagophagia (ice craving) = pica of iron deficiency
exam_pearl: Changing the oral form or frequency never fixes malabsorption; the route must change.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0063; number printed at bottom of p577, content on p578.

stem: A 45-year-old man was admitted to the Intensive Care Unit with fever. He required a vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of more than 65 mm Hg. He is receiving adequate IV fluid resuscitation (see lab result). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: required a vasopressor to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) of more than 65 mm Hg
why_right: The decisive clue is that he "required a vasopressor to maintain MAP > 65 mm Hg" despite "adequate IV fluid resuscitation". Hypotension that persists after fluids and needs vasopressors, in a febrile (infected) patient, defines septic shock, the most severe stage of the sepsis continuum.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sepsis is infection with a dysregulated host response (older model: SIRS plus infection); it does not by itself imply vasopressor dependent hypotension. It would be right if he were infected and unwell but normotensive.
B. Septicemia is an outdated, non defined term for bacteria in the blood with systemic illness; it is not a stage of the sepsis continuum.
D. SIRS is only 2 or more inflammatory criteria (temperature, HR, RR, WBC) without a required infection or hypotension; it fits a post operative inflammatory picture with normal BP.
key_concept:
Sepsis continuum: pick the highest stage the stem proves.
  • SIRS: 2 or more of temp, HR, RR/PaCO2, WBC criteria
  • Sepsis: SIRS (or organ dysfunction) + suspected/confirmed infection
  • Severe sepsis (older term): sepsis + organ dysfunction
  • Septic shock: hypotension needing vasopressors for MAP ≥ 65 despite adequate fluids
  • Sepsis-3 also requires lactate > 2 mmol/L for septic shock
exam_pearl: "Vasopressor despite adequate fluids" is the phrase that upgrades sepsis to septic shock.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0084.

stem: I can't remember the exact details but the description was as it is. Colonoscopy shows linear ulce segmental strictures, and areas of normal mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Linear ulcers, strictures and segmental disease with areas of normal mucosa (skip lesions) are the colonoscopic signature of Crohn's disease. Crohn's inflammation is transmural and patchy, which produces deep linear ulcers (cobblestoning), strictures and fistulae. The question asks for the most specific diagnosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Inflammatory bowel disease is technically true but is an umbrella term covering both Crohn's and UC; when a specific subtype is offered and the findings point to it, choose the specific answer.
C. Ulcerative colitis is continuous inflammation starting in the rectum with no skip areas, superficial ulcers and pseudopolyps; strictures and normal mucosa between affected segments argue against it.
key_concept:
Skip lesions + linear ulcers + strictures = Crohn's.
  • Crohn's: mouth to anus, skip lesions, transmural, cobblestoning, strictures, fistulae, granulomas
  • UC: rectum upward, continuous, mucosal only, pseudopolyps, lead-pipe colon
  • Choose the specific diagnosis over the umbrella term
exam_pearl: Any mention of normal mucosa between diseased areas excludes UC, which never skips.

stem: 5-Year-Old Man Known To Have COPD Presented To The Emergency Department With Increasing Dyspnea, Cough, Expectoration And Fever. Initial Assessment Revealed Fully Conscious Patient With Mild Distress, Central Cyanosis And Bilateral Wheezing On Chest Auscultation. The Patient Was Started On High Flow Oxygen And Salbutamol Nebulizer But 1 Hour Later, His Level Of Consciousness Is Reduced (See Lab Result). Lab Results: ABG HCO3: 36 (Normal: 22-28 mmol/L); ABG PCO2: 9 (Normal: 4.7-6.0 kPa); pH: 7.18 (Normal: 7.36-7.45); ABG PO2: 15 (Normal: 10.6-14.2 kPa). Which Of The Following Is The Best Initial Step In Management?
why_right: A COPD patient put on "high flow oxygen" becomes drowsy "1 hour later" with pH 7.18, PCO2 9 kPa and a supranormal PO2 of 15 kPa. This is oxygen-induced hypercapnia (CO2 narcosis): excess oxygen worsens V/Q mismatch and reduces respiratory drive in a CO2 retainer. The best initial step is to reduce the oxygen (controlled oxygen via Venturi mask) to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92%, then reassess for NIV if acidosis persists.
why_wrong_block:
A. Start mechanical ventilation: needed when respiratory failure persists or the patient cannot protect the airway (unconscious, aspiration risk); here the cause is reversible excess oxygen, so correct that first.
C. Order brain CT scan: right for new focal deficits or suspected stroke/bleed; here the timing after high-flow oxygen and the ABG explain the drowsiness.
D. Give naloxone: right for opioid toxicity (pinpoint pupils, opioid exposure); nothing in the stem suggests opioids.
key_concept:
COPD exacerbation: controlled oxygen, target SpO2 88 to 92%.
  • High PO2 + rising PCO2 + drowsiness = too much oxygen: reduce FiO2
  • Bronchodilators: nebulised SABA + SAMA (ipratropium)
  • Systemic steroid, antibiotics if purulent sputum
  • NIV: alert, cooperative, persistent hypercapnic acidosis despite medical therapy
  • Intubation: unconscious, cannot protect airway, aspiration risk, or NIV failure
exam_pearl: A supranormal PO2 in a hypercapnic COPD patient is the clue: turn the oxygen down before escalating ventilation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Age printed as '5-Year-Old' (likely 50+).

stem: patient with dilated cardiomyopathy on metoprolol develops cardiogenic shock. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Beta blockers are cornerstone therapy in dilated cardiomyopathy (HFrEF) only when the patient is stable. Once "cardiogenic shock" develops, the negative inotropic and chronotropic effect of metoprolol worsens cardiac output, so it must be stopped and the patient supported (inotropes/vasopressors as needed). The beta blocker is reintroduced at a low dose after recovery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Give glucagon as an antidote: right for beta-blocker overdose/toxicity (bradycardia, hypotension after ingestion); here the patient is on a therapeutic dose and decompensated from heart failure.
C. Continue metoprolol and add dobutamine: dobutamine is a reasonable inotrope in cardiogenic shock, but continuing the beta blocker directly opposes it; continuation is right only in stable or mildly decompensated HF without shock.
D. Switch metoprolol to carvedilol: carvedilol is another evidence-based HFrEF beta blocker but is also negatively inotropic and vasodilating, so it would worsen shock.
key_concept:
Beta blockers in HFrEF: start low and titrate when stable; hold in shock.
  • Cardiogenic shock or severe hypotension/low output: stop the beta blocker
  • Mild decompensation without hypotension: usually continue (or reduce dose)
  • Restart at a low dose once stable and euvolaemic
  • Beta-blocker overdose: glucagon is the antidote
  • Evidence-based HFrEF beta blockers: metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol, carvedilol
exam_pearl: Glucagon is for beta-blocker poisoning, not for shock from heart failure in a patient on a normal dose.

stem: Man with history of STD Labs shows trachomatis clamydia
why_right: Labs confirm Chlamydia trachomatis, an intracellular organism that needs an antibiotic with intracellular activity. Azithromycin (single oral dose) is the listed agent that covers chlamydia.
why_wrong_block: A. Ceftriaxone: the treatment for gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae); it does not cover chlamydia. Right when the test shows gonorrhoea, with chlamydia cover added if not excluded.
key_concept:
Urethritis/cervicitis treatment by organism.
  • Chlamydia: doxycycline for 7 days (current preferred) or single-dose azithromycin
  • Azithromycin is preferred in pregnancy
  • Gonorrhoea: IM ceftriaxone
  • Treat partners and test for other STIs
exam_pearl: Ceftriaxone = gonorrhoea; chlamydia needs a macrolide or doxycycline.

stem: A 56-year-old man with chronic renal failure for 5 years presents to the clinic with fatigue for 3 months. His physical examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: Long standing chronic renal failure with fatigue and a stable patient ("physical examination is unremarkable") points to anemia of CKD, caused by erythropoietin deficiency. The expected labs show a normocytic anemia with adequate iron stores (high TSAT and ferritin), so the treatment is an erythropoiesis stimulating agent, subcutaneous erythropoietin.
why_wrong_block:
A. Transfusion is for unstable patients or severe symptomatic anemia; a stable patient with chronic CKD anemia is treated with erythropoietin, which also avoids sensitisation before transplant.
B. IV iron is given when iron stores are low (low TSAT or ferritin) before or alongside erythropoietin; here iron is replete, so there is nothing to correct.
D. Folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anemia; the anemia of CKD is normocytic and due to erythropoietin deficiency.
key_concept:
Anemia of CKD:
  • Cause: reduced renal erythropoietin production
  • Picture: normocytic, normochromic anemia
  • First check iron stores (TSAT, ferritin)
  • Iron low: replace iron first (IV iron often in dialysis patients)
  • Iron replete: erythropoietin, subcutaneous (or IV during hemodialysis)
exam_pearl: Always check iron before erythropoietin: low TSAT or ferritin makes IV iron the answer instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0173.

stem: A patient presented with hypercalcemia. The next step in management was asked. The options included:
why_right: Symptomatic hypercalcaemia causes polyuria and vomiting, leaving the patient volume depleted, which lowers renal calcium excretion. The first step is therefore aggressive IV normal saline to restore volume and promote calciuresis; drugs come after.
why_wrong_block:
A. Calcitonin: works within hours but its effect is modest and wanes quickly (tachyphylaxis); it is an adjunct alongside fluids in severe hypercalcaemia, not the first step.
B. Bisphosphonate: IV zoledronic acid or pamidronate is the step after hydration (onset takes days), especially in malignancy; right as the second step.
C. Denosumab: used for hypercalcaemia of malignancy refractory to bisphosphonates or when renal function prevents bisphosphonate use; not first line.
key_concept:
Hypercalcaemia ladder: fluids first.
  • Step 1: aggressive IV saline
  • Loop diuretic only if volume overload develops after rehydration
  • Step 2: IV bisphosphonate ± calcitonin
  • Refractory or renal impairment: denosumab
  • Lymphoma/granulomatous disease: corticosteroids
  • Renal failure: dialysis
exam_pearl: "Next step" in any hypercalcaemia = IV fluids; bisphosphonate is the next drug, not the first move.

stem: long case but it tells you that through imaging that the patient has a hemorrhagic stroke, he can move his pupils but they are pin point, and he can not speak or move his body, where is the lesion?
highlight_terms_source: can not speak or move his body
why_right: Pontine haemorrhage classically causes pinpoint pupils (loss of descending sympathetic fibres) with quadriplegia and loss of speech. Vertical eye movements are preserved because the midbrain is spared, which is the picture of locked-in syndrome: "can move his pupils/eyes" but "cannot speak or move his body".
why_wrong_block:
B. Medulla: lesions give bulbar signs (dysphagia, dysarthria), crossed sensory loss, vertigo and Horner syndrome (lateral medullary); bilateral pinpoint pupils and locked-in state point to the pons.
C. Basal ganglia: the commonest site of hypertensive haemorrhage, but it causes contralateral hemiparesis with gaze deviation toward the lesion, not pinpoint pupils with quadriplegia.
key_concept:
Haemorrhage localisation by pupils and eyes.
  • Pons: pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia, coma or locked-in state
  • Putamen/basal ganglia: contralateral hemiparesis, eyes deviate toward lesion
  • Thalamus: sensory loss, eyes deviate down and in
  • Cerebellum: ataxia, vomiting, occipital headache
  • Locked-in: only vertical eye movements and blinking preserved
exam_pearl: Pinpoint pupils + coma: think pontine bleed or opioids; with a haemorrhage on imaging it is the pons.

stem: A patient presents with right-sided hemiplegia (power 0/5), left-sided facial palsy, aphasia, and right-hand dominance. He also has facial anesthesia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: Right-sided hemiplegia with aphasia in a right-handed patient places the lesion in the left (dominant) hemisphere; a cortical deficit like aphasia plus contralateral face/arm involvement and sensory loss is the MCA territory. The "left-sided facial palsy" in this recall is most likely a recall slip, since an MCA lesion gives contralateral (right) lower facial weakness.
why_wrong_block:
B. Right MCA stroke: would give left hemiplegia and, in a right-hander, neglect rather than aphasia.
C. Lateral medullary syndrome: ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, vertigo, dysphagia and Horner syndrome; no hemiplegia and no aphasia (no cortical signs).
key_concept:
Aphasia = dominant cortex; side of weakness = opposite hemisphere.
  • MCA: contralateral face and arm > leg weakness and sensory loss, aphasia if dominant, neglect if non-dominant
  • ACA: contralateral leg weakness, incontinence, behaviour change
  • PCA: contralateral homonymous hemianopia
  • Brainstem: crossed signs (ipsilateral cranial nerve, contralateral body), no aphasia
  • Lacunar internal capsule: pure motor face, arm and leg, no aphasia
exam_pearl: Any aphasia rules out a brainstem syndrome: cortical signs put the lesion in the hemisphere.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler repeated 'A) Left MCA stroke' then Answer: A.

stem: 40yo female healthy but recurrent UTI, 4 times in 1 year wants to prevent it. Whats the best clinical based evidence choice to prevent recurrent UTI?
why_right: This recall's key is hydration: for a healthy premenopausal woman with "recurrent UTI, 4 times in 1 year", increasing daily water intake is a simple first-line non-antibiotic measure, and a randomised trial showed fewer recurrences in women with low baseline fluid intake. It is offered before committing a healthy patient to long-term antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
B. Cranberry juice: evidence is mixed and the benefit is small at best; not the best-supported measure.
C. Postcoital hygiene: voiding after intercourse and wiping front to back are common advice but lack trial evidence of benefit.
D. Prophylactic antibiotics: continuous or postcoital antibiotic prophylaxis is the most effective way to reduce recurrences; it is right when behavioural measures fail or UTIs are clearly linked to intercourse.
key_concept:
Recurrent UTI = 2 in 6 months or 3 in 12 months.
  • Confirm with urine culture each episode
  • Behavioural: increase fluid intake
  • Postmenopausal: vaginal oestrogen
  • Intercourse-related: single-dose postcoital antibiotic
  • Otherwise: continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis
exam_pearl: If the stem links UTIs to intercourse, the answer shifts to postcoital single-dose antibiotic.

stem: 28-year-old pregnant woman presents with a history of cough, Green sputum, low-grade fever, night sweats, and weight loss. IGRA is positive (Interferon-gamma release assay). What is the definitive investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
OptC: Sputum for AFB smear and culture
why_right: Cough with sputum, night sweats and weight loss plus a positive IGRA suggest pulmonary TB, but IGRA only proves TB infection (latent or active). The lead-in asks for the "definitive" test: sputum AFB smear with mycobacterial culture. Culture confirms active disease and gives drug sensitivities, and sputum testing is safe in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Chest X-ray: with abdominal shielding it is safe in pregnancy and shows extent (apical infiltrate, cavitation), but imaging cannot confirm the organism; right when asked for the first investigation after a positive screen.
B. Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux): like IGRA it detects infection, not active disease; it adds nothing after a positive IGRA. Right as a screening test for latent TB.
key_concept:
TB tests by purpose.
  • Screening for infection: IGRA or Mantoux (cannot distinguish latent from active)
  • First imaging: chest X-ray
  • Quick microbiology: sputum Ziehl-Neelsen AFB smear, NAAT/PCR
  • Definitive/gold standard: sputum mycobacterial culture (with sensitivities)
  • Suspected active pulmonary TB: airborne isolation first
exam_pearl: "Definitive" or "confirm" TB = culture; IGRA and Mantoux only show infection.

stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic history of heartburn for several years, presented with occasional hematemesis. Upper GI endoscopy revealed intestinal-type metaplasia at the distal esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: intestinal-type metaplasia at the distal esophagus
why_right: Years of chronic heartburn (GERD) with endoscopy showing "intestinal-type metaplasia at the distal esophagus" defines Barrett's oesophagus: normal squamous lining is replaced by columnar epithelium with goblet cells. It is a premalignant change for oesophageal adenocarcinoma and needs surveillance endoscopy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oesophagitis: inflammation and erosions from reflux, without metaplasia; right when endoscopy shows erosions or ulceration only.
B. Mallory-Weiss tear: a mucosal tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction causing haematemesis after forceful vomiting; no metaplasia.
D. Plummer-Vinson syndrome: dysphagia from upper oesophageal webs with iron-deficiency anaemia and glossitis, usually in women; predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma.
key_concept:
Barrett's oesophagus = columnar (intestinal) metaplasia of the distal oesophagus from chronic GERD.
  • Risk factors: long GERD, male, older age, white, obesity, smoking
  • Diagnosis: endoscopy + biopsy showing intestinal metaplasia
  • Treatment: PPI; surveillance endoscopy
  • Dysplasia: endoscopic ablation/resection
  • Cancer risk: adenocarcinoma (not squamous)
exam_pearl: Metaplasia = Barrett's; webs + iron deficiency = Plummer-Vinson; vomiting then blood = Mallory-Weiss.

stem: Old male presented with left side body weakness resolve completely after 20 minutes, brain ct normal, carotid ultrasounds show stenosis > 55%. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Weakness that "resolved completely after 20 minutes" with a normal CT is a TIA, and the carotid scan points to large-artery atherosclerosis, not a cardiac embolus. Every TIA from an atherosclerotic source gets antiplatelet therapy straight away, so aspirin is the immediate next step while the stenosis is assessed for surgery. Nothing in the stem (no AF, no valve disease) justifies anticoagulation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Apixaban is for cardioembolic TIA, mainly atrial fibrillation; there is no AF here, and anticoagulation does not beat antiplatelets for carotid disease.
C. Warfarin is also reserved for a cardioembolic source such as AF or a mechanical valve; it is not used for carotid atherosclerosis.
