D. Endarterectomy has its clearest benefit in symptomatic 70-99% stenosis in a fit patient; at 50-69% the benefit is smaller and selective. Either way it is arranged within days to weeks, and aspirin is started immediately, so surgery is not the first step.
key_concept:
TIA: antiplatelet now, then target the source.
  • Carotid source: aspirin, statin and risk factor control; endarterectomy for significant symptomatic stenosis
  • AF source: anticoagulation (DOAC or warfarin), not aspirin
  • Initial imaging after a TIA: brain CT, then carotid duplex
  • Ischemic stroke after the thrombolysis window: aspirin for secondary prevention
exam_pearl: If the stem adds AF (irregular pulse or ECG), the answer flips to anticoagulation. If it says severe stenosis (≥70%), endarterectomy becomes the key.

stem: Senna syrup is used to treat chronic constipation, which of the following is considered a serious adverse effect / side effect ?
why_right: Senna is a stimulant laxative. Long-term or excessive use causes chronic diarrheal fluid loss, which wastes potassium. The resulting hypokalemia is the serious adverse effect: it causes weakness and arrhythmias, and it can worsen the constipation itself by causing colonic atony. The other listed effects are common and expected but not dangerous.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diarrhea is the most common side effect and an extension of the drug's action. It matters mainly because it leads to electrolyte loss, which is the serious harm.
B. Abdominal cramps are a frequent, benign effect of stimulant laxatives and usually settle with dose reduction.
D. "Synergic effect" is not an adverse effect; it describes how drugs interact and is a distractor.
key_concept:
Laxative classes and their key toxicity:
  • Stimulant (senna, bisacodyl): cramps, diarrhea; serious = hypokalemia and electrolyte loss with chronic use
  • Osmotic (lactulose, PEG): bloating and flatulence
  • Bulk (psyllium): first line for uncomplicated chronic constipation; needs fluid
  • Hypokalemia: weakness, ileus, flattened T waves, arrhythmia
exam_pearl: When a question asks for the "serious" side effect, pick the dangerous metabolic or organ effect, not the common nuisance one.

stem: A 26-year-old male presents for evaluation of a systolic murmur noted during a routine checkup. He is asymptomatic, with no history of chest pain, dyspnea, or palpitations. On auscultation, a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Bedside maneuvers: The murmur increases with standing or Valsalva. The murmur decreases with handgrip or squatting. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur
why_right: A young asymptomatic man with a "mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur" at the apex has the signature of mitral valve prolapse. The maneuvers confirm it. Standing or Valsalva make the LV smaller, so the leaflets prolapse earlier and the murmur gets longer and louder. Squatting or handgrip enlarge the LV, so the click moves later and the murmur softens.
why_wrong_block:
A. Degenerative (primary) MR is the broad category, and MVP is its commonest cause; once MR is significant it gives a holosystolic apical murmur that softens on standing or Valsalva and gets louder with handgrip. The isolated click plus late systolic murmur that grows on standing names the specific lesion, MVP.
B. Secondary MR comes from LV dilation or ischemic remodelling in a diseased heart (cardiomyopathy, prior MI), not in a healthy 26-year-old. It is holosystolic and has no click.
C. Functional MR is another name for secondary MR from a dilated ventricle or annulus. It has the same holosystolic pattern without a click and needs underlying heart disease.
key_concept:
Maneuvers for systolic murmurs (Valsalva or standing / squatting / handgrip):
  • MVP: ↑ / ↓ / ↓ (click moves earlier on standing)
  • HOCM: ↑ / ↓ / ↓ (harsh ejection murmur, no click)
  • MR: ↓ / ↑ / ↑
  • AS: ↓ / ↑ / ↓
exam_pearl: MVP and HOCM share the same maneuver pattern. The click and the apical late systolic murmur mean MVP; an ejection murmur at the left sternal border with syncope means HOCM.

stem: A Patient With Acute exacerbation COPD they literally gave him everything for management of COPD (Nebs, SABA, SAMA, ABX) but no O2 given. He does not have confusion or any CNS symptoms or absent gag Or Any Indication For Intubation. ABG: CO2 65 kp, O2 55 kp, Ph 7.18, O2 Sat: 70%
why_right: This recall's key is intubation because the gas shows decompensated hypercapnic respiratory failure: pH 7.18, raised CO2 and severe hypoxemia ("O2 Sat 70%") despite full bronchodilator and antibiotic therapy. Respiratory failure is one of the listed triggers for intubation in a COPD exacerbation. The source treats this degree of acidemia and hypoxemia as too severe to rely on noninvasive support. The units are almost certainly mmHg, not kPa.
why_wrong_block:
A. High-flow nasal cannula improves oxygenation but does not remove CO2 reliably. Uncontrolled oxygen in a CO2 retainer can also worsen hypercapnia. It is not the answer for hypercapnic acidosis.
B. Positive pressure (noninvasive) ventilation is for an alert, cooperative patient with hypercapnic acidosis despite bronchodilators and steroids. It is the step this key bypasses because the source judges the failure too severe.
C. Tracheostomy is a later procedure for prolonged ventilation or failure to wean. It is never the acute step in an exacerbation.
key_concept:
Acute COPD exacerbation ladder:
  • Controlled O2 (Venturi), target SpO2 88-92%
  • Nebulised SABA + SAMA, systemic steroid, antibiotic if infective
  • NIV: alert, cooperative, hypercapnic acidosis despite medical therapy
  • Intubation: unconscious, cannot protect airway or aspiration risk, NIV failure, or respiratory failure
exam_pearl: Check whether controlled oxygen has been given. A stem saying "no O2 given" and "no indication for intubation" usually points to O2 and NIV, so read the key and the stem carefully.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Question is a screenshot; typed answer line: D. Elective intubation and mechanical ventilation.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents with insomnia, irritability and palpitation for 3 months. He is known to have hypertension, depression and atrial fibrillation. He is on amiodarone, fluoxetine and enalopril. Clinically, he is unremarkable. Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, Heart rate 76 /min, Oxygen saturation 95 %. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: Insomnia, irritability and palpitations for 3 months are classic hyperthyroid symptoms. He is on amiodarone, which is iodine-rich and can cause thyrotoxicosis (or hypothyroidism). The exam and vitals are unremarkable (HR 76), so the next step is to measure free T4 and TSH before changing any drug.
why_wrong_block:
A. Propranolol would control adrenergic symptoms once thyrotoxicosis is confirmed, but treating before confirming the diagnosis is premature. His heart rate is already 76.
C. Fluoxetine can cause insomnia and agitation, but swapping the antidepressant ignores the more dangerous and testable cause, amiodarone-induced thyroid dysfunction.
D. Psychiatric referral is for a primary psychiatric cause. An organic, drug-related cause must be excluded first.
key_concept:
Amiodarone monitoring and toxicity:
  • Thyroid: hypo- or hyperthyroidism; check TFTs at baseline and periodically
  • Lungs: pulmonary fibrosis
  • Liver: raised transaminases
  • Skin and eyes: blue-grey skin, photosensitivity, corneal deposits
  • New anxiety, insomnia or palpitations on amiodarone: check TSH and free T4 first
exam_pearl: When a patient on amiodarone develops new symptoms, test for drug toxicity (thyroid, lung, liver) before blaming another drug or a psychiatric cause.

stem: 66-year-old man with hypertension comes to the clinic for a follow-up. He is currently taking a combination of losartan and amlodipine, which is failing to keep his blood pressure within target. Examination is unremarkable. His blood test and renal function profile were within the normal limits. What is the most appropriate next step assuming he has no relevant contraindications?
highlight_terms_source: failing to keep his blood pressure within target
why_right: He is uncontrolled on an ARB (losartan) plus a CCB (amlodipine), which is step 2. Step 3 adds a thiazide-like diuretic, giving ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic. With normal renal function and electrolytes and no contraindications, indapamide MR 1.5 mg once daily is the correct addition.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ramipril is an ACE inhibitor. Combining it with an ARB (dual RAAS blockade) raises the risk of hyperkalemia and AKI without benefit.
B. Atenolol is a step 4 option for resistant hypertension (if K+ is above 4.5) or for a compelling indication such as angina. It is not the third drug.
C. Doxazosin, an alpha-blocker, is also a step 4 add-on for resistant hypertension. It is not used at step 3.
key_concept:
Hypertension drug ladder:
  • Step 1: ACEi/ARB (age under 55 or diabetic) or CCB (age over 55 or African/Caribbean origin)
  • Step 2: ACEi/ARB + CCB or thiazide-like diuretic
  • Step 3: ACEi/ARB + CCB + thiazide-like diuretic
  • Step 4: spironolactone if K+ < 4.5; alpha- or beta-blocker if K+ > 4.5
  • Never combine ACEi with ARB
exam_pearl: If the patient were already on all three step 3 drugs, the answer would move to spironolactone (or an alpha/beta-blocker depending on potassium).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer given as 'D (MG)'.

stem: Old Patient came with Cirrhosis and massive hematemesis, became drowsy, and blood oozing out from his mouth. What is the next step of management?
highlight_terms_source: blood oozing out from his mouth
why_right: In any upper GI bleed, the sequence starts with A for airway. This cirrhotic patient is "drowsy" (encephalopathy or shock) with "blood oozing out from his mouth", so he cannot protect his airway and is at high risk of aspiration. Endotracheal intubation secures the airway first and also makes urgent endoscopy safe. Transfusion, octreotide and endoscopy all follow.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood transfusion is part of resuscitation (restrictive target, Hb about 7), but with an unprotected airway and active hematemesis, airway comes before circulation.
C. Octreotide is the right vasoactive drug for suspected variceal bleeding and should start early. It does not address imminent aspiration in a drowsy patient.
D. Urgent endoscopy with band ligation is the definitive step, but it is done after resuscitation. In a drowsy patient with massive hematemesis, it is done only after intubation.
key_concept:
Variceal bleed sequence:
  • Airway: intubate if drowsy, massive hematemesis or aspiration risk
  • Two large-bore IVs, fluids, restrictive transfusion
  • IV octreotide (vasoactive) + IV ceftriaxone (reduces mortality)
  • Endoscopy: band ligation (sclerotherapy as alternative)
  • Failure: balloon tamponade, then TIPS; after: nonselective beta-blocker + banding
exam_pearl: A stable, alert cirrhotic with hematemesis gets fluids, octreotide and then endoscopy. Add drowsiness or blood pooling in the mouth and the answer becomes intubation.

stem: A middle-aged man with diabetes mellitus is on metformin and aspirin. His labs show elevated creatinine and high BUN. He is planning to travel and asks about prophylaxis for traveler’s diarrhea. Which of the following is the most appropriate option?
why_right: Routine prophylaxis for traveler's diarrhea is not recommended; travelers are advised on food and water hygiene and given standby treatment instead. In this patient the only drug options are unsafe. Bismuth subsalicylate adds salicylate on top of his "aspirin", and both bismuth and salicylate accumulate when "creatinine and BUN" are raised. Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis has adverse effects and drives resistance. So no prophylactic medication is the best choice.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bismuth subsalicylate is the classic nonantibiotic prophylaxis for healthy travelers. Here it adds salicylate to aspirin (toxicity, bleeding) and is avoided in renal impairment.
B. Fluoroquinolones are not used for routine prophylaxis because of tendon, CNS and QT effects, C. difficile risk and resistance. They are for treating moderate to severe diarrhea, and they need dose adjustment in renal impairment.
D. Probiotics have no consistent evidence of preventing traveler's diarrhea, so they are not recommended.
key_concept:
Traveler's diarrhea:
  • Prevention: food and water precautions; routine drug prophylaxis is not advised
  • Bismuth subsalicylate: avoid with aspirin or anticoagulants, in renal impairment, children and pregnancy; causes black stool and tongue
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis: only selected high-risk hosts, and not with fluoroquinolones
  • Treatment: oral rehydration ± loperamide; antibiotic (azithromycin) for severe or dysenteric illness
  • On metformin: hold during significant dehydrating diarrhea (lactic acidosis risk)
exam_pearl: A patient on aspirin plus renal impairment is the clue that rules out bismuth subsalicylate.
compiler_note: Compiler note: We need the exact number of Cr level and BUN, If severe CKD or ESKD then answer is A.

stem: A 38-year-old woman presented with a 7-weeks of frequent, loose and bloody bowel movements that associated with campy abdominal and rectal pain. She has family history of crohn's disease. Stool analysis is negaive (see lab results). Blood pressure 110/70 mmH, Heart rate 76 /min, Temperature 36.6 °C. Test / Result / Normal Values: RBC 9.2 (4.2-5.4 × 10¹²/L female); Hb 111 (120-160 g/L female); HCT 0.41 (0.37-0.48 female); MCH 27 (28-33 pg/cell); MCHC 330 (320-360 g/L); MCV 77 (80-95 fL); Platelets count 220 (150-400 × 10⁹/L); C-reactive protein 22 (<8.2 mg/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in establishing diagnosis?
why_right: This recall's key (MG) is upper GI endoscopy. Seven weeks of bloody diarrhea with cramps and rectal pain, a "family history of Crohn's", microcytic anemia (MCV 77) and a raised CRP (22) with negative stool studies point to organic inflammatory bowel disease, not a functional disorder. The diagnosis is made by endoscopy with biopsy, and in suspected Crohn's disease the upper GI tract is also examined to map involvement. Upper GI endoscopy is the only endoscopic option listed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anorectal manometry tests sphincter function in fecal incontinence or dyssynergic defecation. It does not diagnose an inflammatory cause of bloody diarrhea.
C. Celiac testing belongs in the workup of chronic non-bloody diarrhea or suspected IBS. Celiac disease rarely causes bloody stools with rectal pain.
D. Fecal calprotectin helps separate IBD from IBS when it is unclear whether the cause is organic. It only shows intestinal inflammation, which blood, anemia and a raised CRP already show here, and it cannot establish the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Suspected IBD workup:
  • Stool culture and C. difficile to exclude infection
  • CBC, CRP, iron studies; fecal calprotectin to triage IBD vs IBS
  • Diagnosis: ileocolonoscopy with biopsies
  • Suspected Crohn's: also assess upper GI tract and small bowel (MR or CT enterography)
  • Celiac serology: for IBS-like or non-bloody chronic diarrhea
exam_pearl: Bloody diarrhea with anemia and a raised CRP is already organic disease, so go to endoscopy. Calprotectin and celiac testing fit the IBS-like stem without blood.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B. Upper GI endoscopy (MG).

stem: Young male presented with vomiting of blood, he was heavy alcohol consumption, stable; endoscopy show esophageal varices. What is the cause of varices:
why_right: Esophageal varices are portosystemic collaterals that form when portal pressure rises. In a "heavy alcohol" drinker the cause is alcoholic cirrhosis, which raises intrahepatic resistance and causes portal hypertension. The blood is then diverted through the left gastric to esophageal veins, which dilate and bleed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acute pancreatitis does not cause esophageal varices. Chronic pancreatitis can cause splenic vein thrombosis, but that gives isolated gastric (fundal) varices, not esophageal ones.
C. Essential (systemic) hypertension affects arterial pressure and has no effect on the portal venous system, so it does not cause varices.
D. Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein outflow obstruction) does cause portal hypertension and varices. It typically presents with abdominal pain, hepatomegaly and ascites, often in a thrombophilic state. Here the alcohol history points to cirrhosis, and the question asks for the mechanism common to all varices.
key_concept:
Portal hypertension causes:
  • Prehepatic: portal or splenic vein thrombosis (splenic gives isolated gastric varices)
  • Intrahepatic: cirrhosis (alcohol, viral), schistosomiasis
  • Posthepatic: Budd-Chiari, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis
  • Consequences: varices, ascites (SAAG ≥1.1), splenomegaly, caput medusae
exam_pearl: Isolated gastric fundal varices with a normal portal vein after pancreatitis means splenic vein thrombosis, and the treatment is splenectomy.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a known diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with polyuria and polydipsia. He is taking vitamin D supplements for a previous deficiency. Family history: relative with type 1 DM. Labs: Elevated PTH; Normal calcium; HbA1c: 8%; Normal urine osmolality and serum osmolality; Elevated C-peptide: 0.09 ng/mL (Low). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Normal urine osmolality and serum osmolality
why_right: A young adult ("30-year-old") labelled as type 2 with a family history of type 1 DM and a low C-peptide (0.09 ng/mL) has absent endogenous insulin secretion, which means autoimmune beta-cell failure, i.e. type 1 DM (often slow-onset, LADA-like, in adults). HbA1c 8% plus polyuria and polydipsia confirms hyperglycemia as the cause of the symptoms. The stem says "elevated" C-peptide but the value and its "(Low)" label are the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diabetes insipidus gives polyuria with dilute urine (low urine osmolality) and often high serum osmolality; here osmolalities are normal and HbA1c is high, so the polyuria is glycemic.
C. Type 2 DM has preserved or high C-peptide from insulin resistance; a low C-peptide argues against the existing label. T2DM would fit an older, obese patient with normal or raised C-peptide.
D. PTH is high with normal calcium in a patient with previous vitamin D deficiency, which is secondary hyperparathyroidism, not a cause of these symptoms. Primary hyperparathyroidism causes polyuria through high calcium.
key_concept:
C-peptide separates insulin-deficient from insulin-resistant diabetes.
  • Low C-peptide: type 1 DM / LADA (adult-onset autoimmune)
  • Normal or high C-peptide: type 2 DM
  • Polyuria + low urine osmolality: diabetes insipidus
  • Polyuria + high calcium + high PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism
  • High PTH + normal or low calcium + low vitamin D: secondary hyperparathyroidism
exam_pearl: A "type 2" patient who is young, non-responsive or has low C-peptide is type 1 (LADA) until proven otherwise; confirm with GAD antibodies.

stem: Has Fhx of DM T2, A1c 8 (I guess), Fasting Blood Glucose 9 (I guess), BMI 34. Which is the first line treatment here:
why_right: New type 2 DM with "A1c 8", fasting glucose 9 and BMI 34, asked for "first line" treatment: lifestyle modification plus metformin is the standard starting therapy when HbA1c at diagnosis is roughly 7.5 to 10%. Metformin is weight-neutral, does not cause hypoglycemia on its own, and is cheap and well established.
why_wrong_block: A. Liraglutide (GLP-1 agonist) is an injectable add-on when metformin is not enough or when weight loss or established cardiovascular disease drives the choice; it is not the classic first-line drug for an uncomplicated new patient.
key_concept:
Initial T2DM treatment by HbA1c at diagnosis:
  • Below 7.5%: lifestyle alone
  • 7.5 to 10%: lifestyle + metformin
  • Above 10% or symptomatic catabolic state: insulin
  • Established ASCVD, heart failure or CKD: add GLP-1 agonist or SGLT2 inhibitor
  • Sulfonylureas: avoid as first line in obesity (weight gain, hypoglycemia)
exam_pearl: Obesity alone does not replace metformin as first line in exam questions; GLP-1 agonists come in for comorbid cardiovascular disease or inadequate control.

stem: A 20-year-old man with a history of high liver function test in the past presents, with tremors and dysarthria and dyskinesia. Slit-lamp examination reveals a greenish-brown ring at comeoscleral junction. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 20-year-old with previous raised liver tests, extrapyramidal signs (tremor, dysarthria, dyskinesia) and a greenish-brown ring at the corneoscleral junction on slit lamp (Kayser-Fleischer ring) has Wilson disease. Copper accumulates in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea, producing exactly this liver + brain + eye triad in a young patient.
why_wrong_block:
A. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes liver disease with early panacinar (lower lobe) emphysema, but no movement disorder and no corneal ring.
B. Hepatic hemangioma is a benign vascular lesion, usually an incidental imaging finding with no neurological or eye signs.
C. Hemochromatosis (iron overload) gives liver disease, bronze skin, diabetes, arthropathy and cardiomyopathy, usually in middle age; it does not cause Kayser-Fleischer rings or extrapyramidal signs.
key_concept:
Young patient + liver disease + neuropsychiatric signs = Wilson disease.
  • Defect: impaired biliary copper excretion (ATP7B), autosomal recessive
  • Eyes: Kayser-Fleischer ring (slit lamp)
  • Labs: low ceruloplasmin, high 24-h urine copper
  • Treatment: chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc
exam_pearl: Liver disease plus a movement disorder or psychiatric change in a young person: check ceruloplasmin; hemochromatosis instead pairs liver disease with diabetes and bronze skin in middle age.

stem: Another question about gram negative diplococci and what is the disses this Bactria cause
why_right: Gram-negative diplococci are Neisseria species; in a meningitis or sepsis setting this is Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), the classic cause of meningitis with a petechial or purpuric rash. (The other Gram-negative diplococcus, N. gonorrhoeae, causes urethritis, cervicitis and septic arthritis.)
why_wrong_block:
B. Group A streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is a Gram-positive coccus in chains, causing pharyngitis, impetigo, cellulitis and rheumatic fever.
C. Group B streptococcus (S. agalactiae) is a Gram-positive coccus in chains, the main cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
key_concept:
Gram stain shortcuts in meningitis:
  • Gram-negative diplococci: Neisseria meningitidis
  • Gram-positive diplococci (lancet-shaped): Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Gram-negative coccobacilli: Haemophilus influenzae
  • Gram-positive rods: Listeria (neonates, elderly, immunocompromised)
  • Gram-positive cocci in chains: group B strep (neonates)
exam_pearl: Gram-positive diplococci = pneumococcus; Gram-NEGATIVE diplococci = meningococcus. The stain colour is the whole question.

stem: Man with ALL started chemotherapy and he developed fever after 8 days : I am sure it was 8 days .
why_right: Fever in a patient with ALL about 8 days after chemotherapy (the neutrophil nadir period) is febrile neutropenia until proven otherwise, a medical emergency. After a septic screen, start empirical broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (an antipseudomonal agent such as piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime or meropenem) immediately, without waiting for cultures.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance ignores a potentially fatal infection; neutropenic patients may deteriorate to septic shock within hours and show few localizing signs.
C. Antifungal therapy is added only if fever persists beyond about 4 to 7 days despite antibiotics; it is not part of the initial empirical regimen.
key_concept:
Febrile neutropenia ladder:
  • Step 1: cultures (blood, urine, sputum) + immediate IV broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotic
  • Add vancomycin: sepsis, catheter or skin infection, MRSA, pneumonia
  • Persistent fever after 4 to 7 days: add antifungal
  • Do not delay antibiotics for results
exam_pearl: "Antibiotic AND antifungal" is the trap; the antifungal comes later for persistent fever, not on day one.

stem: blood transfusion after transfusion following sudden breathlessness. How to prevent in future?
key_concept:
Match the breathless transfusion reaction to its prevention.
  • Allergic (urticaria, wheeze): antihistamine premedication
  • Anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency: washed or IgA-deficient products
  • TACO (hypertension, raised JVP, edema): slower rate, diuretic
  • TRALI (hypotension, fever, bilateral infiltrates within 6 h): supportive; exclude implicated donor
  • Hypothermia with massive transfusion: blood warmer
exam_pearl: Breathlessness with hypertension and fluid overload points to TACO (slow it down); with urticaria or wheeze it is allergic (antihistamine).
compiler_note:
Compiler note: No answer marked on the numbered recall. The following 'Q:' (skin rash and facial flushes after transfusion, Answer: B) is carded separately.
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Case about a 30-40 man getting blood transfusion in the ER and minutes after he got skin rash and facial flushes: How to prevent this:
OptD: Matching the recipient with the donor ethnicity
why_right: Skin rash and facial flushing starting minutes after a transfusion is a mild allergic (urticarial) reaction to donor plasma proteins, mediated by histamine release. For a patient who has had such reactions, pre-medication with an antihistamine before future transfusions is the preventive step this recall keys.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pushing the bag quickly does nothing to prevent allergy and risks circulatory overload; a slow rate is used to prevent TACO.
C. Warming blood prevents hypothermia and arrhythmias in rapid or massive transfusion, not allergic skin reactions.
D. Donor ethnicity is irrelevant; compatibility depends on ABO/Rh and antibody screening, and these do not prevent plasma-protein allergic reactions.
key_concept:
Transfusion reactions and prevention:
  • Urticaria, flushing, itch: allergic; antihistamine (premedicate next time)
  • Anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency): washed or IgA-deficient products
  • Fever, chills (febrile non-hemolytic): leukoreduced blood, antipyretic
  • Fever, hypotension, hemoglobinuria: acute hemolytic (ABO mismatch); stop transfusion
  • Rapid or massive transfusion: blood warmer
exam_pearl: Rash only, stable vitals: pause, give antihistamine, may resume; add hypotension or wheeze and it is anaphylaxis, stop and give adrenaline.
compiler_note:
Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1263).
Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant under 2477.

stem: 25-year-old male came recently from India, presented to ER with RUQ pain, Night sweats, malaise, fever. US showed: right lobe Liver collection, Hypoechoic CT Finding: Thick walled abscess without septations. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
why_right: A young man recently from India (endemic area) with fever, RUQ pain and night sweats and a single hypoechoic right-lobe collection without septations is the classic picture of amoebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica). Diagnosis is supported by amoebic serology, and treatment is metronidazole without routine drainage.
why_wrong_block:
B. Pyogenic abscess is favoured in an older patient with biliary disease, diabetes or recent abdominal sepsis, often multiple lesions; travel from an endemic area points to amoebic.
C. Hydatid cyst (Echinococcus, contact with dogs or livestock) shows a cyst with daughter cysts, septations or calcification and is usually less acutely febrile; here there are no septations.
D. Tuberculous liver abscess is rare and usually accompanies disseminated or miliary TB; night sweats alone do not make it the most likely diagnosis.
key_concept:
Liver collection by setting:
  • Young male, travel to India or Mexico, single right-lobe lesion: amoebic; metronidazole
  • Elderly, biliary disease or diabetes, multiple lesions: pyogenic; antibiotics + drainage
  • Farmer or dog contact, daughter cysts, septations, calcification: hydatid; albendazole ± surgery
exam_pearl: Amoebic abscess is treated medically first (metronidazole); do not aspirate a suspected hydatid cyst casually because of the anaphylaxis risk.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis is treated with prednisolone 60 mg orally once daily for an acute exacerbation. She is instructed to continue the treatment for a short period and then gradually taper the dose. However, the patient fails to follow the tapering instructions and continues taking prednisolone 60 mg daily for several days. She is subsequently found dead at home. Which of the following is the most likely cause of death?
why_right: This recall's key is hemorrhagic stroke, on the reasoning that sustained high-dose prednisolone (60 mg daily) raises blood pressure and causes fluid retention and hyperglycemia, which can precipitate an intracerebral bleed in a 60-year-old. The stem stresses that she kept taking the full dose rather than stopping, which is why the source did not choose adrenal insufficiency.
why_wrong_block:
A. High-dose steroids raise peptic ulcer risk mainly when combined with NSAIDs and can mask perforation signs, but perforation usually presents with acute abdominal pain and peritonitis rather than unexplained sudden death within days; the source keyed the vascular event instead.
B. Steroids treat vasculitis rather than cause it; acute cerebral vasculitis is not a recognized consequence of steroid excess.
D. Acute adrenal insufficiency follows abrupt withdrawal after prolonged therapy or a stressor without dose cover; a patient still taking 60 mg daily has ample glucocorticoid.
E. Steroid-induced pancreatitis is rare and would not typically cause sudden unwitnessed death within days.
key_concept:
Steroid danger depends on direction:
  • Stopping abruptly after prolonged use: adrenal crisis (hypotension, hypoglycemia, death)
  • Continuing high doses: hypertension, hyperglycemia, infection, peptic ulcer/perforation (masked), psychosis
  • Taper is needed after about 3 weeks of supraphysiological dosing
exam_pearl: Read whether the patient STOPPED or CONTINUED the steroid: stopping = adrenal crisis; continuing = steroid excess complications.

stem: A ]age not recalled[ male presented to the emergency department with icterus and jaundice. Serology showed: Hepatitis A: • Anti-HAV IgM — positive • Anti-HAV IgG — positive. Hepatitis B: • Anti-HBs (surface antibody) — positive • HBsAg (surface antigen) — negative • Anti-HBc (core antibody) — negative • HBeAg (e antigen) — negative. What is the diagnosis?
OptC: Acute hepatitis A with immunization against hepatitis B
OptD: Acute hepatitis A with previous hepatitis B infection
why_right: Anti-HAV IgM positive means acute hepatitis A, explaining the jaundice (IgG can co-exist as the response evolves). For hepatitis B, anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative and HBsAg negative is the pattern of vaccination: immunity without ever meeting the virus.
why_wrong_block:
A. Correct as far as it goes, but it ignores the hepatitis B panel; the best answer must also interpret the anti-HBs positive / anti-HBc negative immune status.
B. Chronic hepatitis B requires persistent HBsAg positivity with anti-HBc IgG; both are negative here.
D. Previous natural HBV infection leaves anti-HBs plus anti-HBc; anti-HBc is negative, so immunity came from the vaccine.
key_concept:
Hepatitis B serology:
  • Anti-HBs only: vaccinated
  • Anti-HBs + anti-HBc IgG: past infection, recovered
  • HBsAg + anti-HBc IgM: acute HBV
  • HBsAg + anti-HBc IgG (over 6 months): chronic HBV
  • Hepatitis A: IgM = acute; IgG alone = past infection or vaccine
exam_pearl: Anti-HBc is the marker of real exposure; if it is negative, any anti-HBs comes from the vaccine.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 5-month history of fatigue. She takes no medication. Her examination is unremarkable (see lab results). Tsh 14, Normal t 4, T.cholestrol 5.3, Ldl 2.7 ??, Tg slightly high. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's dyslipidemia?
why_right: The labs show a TSH of 14 with a normal T4, which is subclinical hypothyroidism, and the 5 months of "fatigue" fits an underactive thyroid. Her lipids are only mildly abnormal, and hypothyroidism is a recognised secondary cause of raised cholesterol and triglycerides. The lead-in asks how to treat this patient's dyslipidemia, so you treat the cause: thyroxine, with TSH above 10 being a standard threshold to start replacement. The lipids are then rechecked once she is euthyroid.
why_wrong_block:
A. Statin: first line for primary dyslipidemia or established ASCVD, but here the lipid change is secondary to hypothyroidism, and statins in untreated hypothyroidism also carry a higher myopathy risk.
B. Fibrate: used mainly for markedly high triglycerides (pancreatitis risk); her triglycerides are only slightly high and will likely improve with thyroid replacement.
C. Niacin: no longer a routine lipid agent because it adds no outcome benefit and has many side effects; never the answer for secondary dyslipidemia.
key_concept:
Dyslipidemia + abnormal thyroid tests: treat the thyroid first, then reassess lipids.
  • High TSH + low T4: overt hypothyroidism, treat with levothyroxine
  • High TSH + normal T4: subclinical; treat if TSH ≥10 or symptomatic
  • Isolated primary dyslipidemia: statin
  • Secondary causes to exclude: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, diabetes, cholestasis, drugs
  • Recheck TSH about 6 weeks after starting or changing the dose
exam_pearl: Fatigue plus a lipid question with thyroid labs in the table: the answer is thyroxine, not a statin.

stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman visits the clinic for regular follow-up. She is asymptomatic. She is in her 30th week of pregnancy. Her physical examination reveals a mid-systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border. The murmur radiates to carotids. No diastolic murmur is heard. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: mid-systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border
why_right: A mid-systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border (aortic area) that radiates to the carotids is the classic aortic stenosis murmur. Pregnancy does produce flow murmurs, but carotid radiation is a pathological feature that a benign flow murmur does not have. In a young woman the likely cause is a congenital (often bicuspid) valve, and she needs an echocardiogram.
why_wrong_block:
B. Mitral stenosis: a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap; this card has a systolic murmur and states no diastolic murmur.
C. Tricuspid stenosis: also a diastolic rumble, heard at the lower left sternal border and louder on inspiration; not a systolic murmur radiating to the carotids.
D. Physiologic murmur of pregnancy: a soft systolic flow murmur, usually at the left sternal border, that does not radiate to the carotids; right when the murmur is soft, localised and the patient is asymptomatic without carotid radiation.
key_concept:
Step 1: systolic or diastolic. Step 2: site and radiation.
  • Systolic ejection, right upper sternal border, radiates to carotids: aortic stenosis
  • Holosystolic at apex, radiates to axilla: mitral regurgitation
  • Mid-diastolic apical rumble with opening snap: mitral stenosis
  • Early decrescendo diastolic at left sternal border: aortic regurgitation
  • Pregnancy flow murmur: soft, systolic, no radiation, no diastolic component
  • Any diastolic murmur or carotid radiation in pregnancy: get an echo
exam_pearl: Pregnancy is a distractor; the carotid radiation makes it organic aortic stenosis, not a flow murmur.

stem: A 77-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension presents with a 6-months history of fatigue and dyspnea on exertion. He denies edema, orthopnea, chest pain and palpitations. His only medication is hydrochlorothiazide (25 mg) once daily. On examination, he has a grade 2/6 midsystolic ejection murmur, which is loudest at the right upper sternal border. An S4 is heard at the apex, there is no S3. His lungs are clear and there is no peripheral edema. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: loudest at the right upper sternal border
why_right: A midsystolic ejection murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border in a 77-year-old is aortic stenosis until proven otherwise, most often from age-related calcific degeneration. The S4 at the apex reflects a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle from pressure overload (worsened by his poorly controlled hypertension). Exertional dyspnea and fatigue are early AS symptoms, and the absence of an S3, edema and crackles shows he is not yet in overt failure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aortic regurgitation: an early decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border with a wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse; this murmur is systolic.
B. Mitral regurgitation: a holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, often with an S3 from volume overload; not an ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border.
D. Mitral stenosis: a mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap, usually rheumatic and in younger patients; this murmur is systolic and at the aortic area.
key_concept:
Elderly + ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border = calcific aortic stenosis.
  • S4: stiff LV from pressure overload (AS, hypertension)
  • S3: volume overload or systolic failure (MR, dilated LV)
  • AS triad of symptoms: exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope
  • Severe AS signs: slow rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft S2
  • Initial test for a new murmur: transthoracic echo
exam_pearl: Systolic at the base points to AS; systolic at the apex radiating to the axilla points to MR.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the clinic with progressive shortness of breath on exertion for 8 months. He has no history of chest pain or other systemic manifestations. Physical examination reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border that is augmented when sitting forward (see reports). Chest radiography: Cardiomegaly. ECG: Left ventricular hypertrophy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border
why_right: The decisive sign is an early diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder sitting forward, the classic decrescendo murmur of aortic regurgitation. The chronic volume overload explains 8 months of progressive exertional dyspnea, cardiomegaly on chest X-ray (LV dilatation) and LVH on ECG.
why_wrong_block:
A. Aortic stenosis gives a crescendo decrescendo systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids, not a diastolic murmur.
B. Mitral stenosis gives a low pitched mid diastolic rumble at the apex (best in left lateral position) with an opening snap, not an early diastolic murmur at the base.
D. Mitral regurgitation gives a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla.
key_concept:
First decide systolic vs diastolic, then location and maneuver.
  • Early diastolic decrescendo, left sternal border, sitting forward in expiration: AR (or PR)
  • Mid diastolic rumble with opening snap at apex: MS
  • Systolic ejection to carotids: AS
  • Holosystolic apex to axilla: MR
  • AR signs: wide pulse pressure, collapsing pulse, displaced apex, Austin Flint murmur
exam_pearl: An apical diastolic rumble in a patient with AR may be an Austin Flint murmur, not true mitral stenosis.

stem: A 33-year-old man presented with shortness of breath, orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. Examination revealed collapsing pulse and wide pulse pressure. Early diastolic murmur over left sternal border and pistol-shot sound heard over femoral arteries. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: The peripheral signs are textbook for a large regurgitant aortic volume: collapsing (water hammer) pulse, wide pulse pressure and pistol-shot sounds over the femorals. Add an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border and the diagnosis is aortic regurgitation. Orthopnea and PND show the volume-loaded left ventricle is now failing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coarctation of aorta: upper limb hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses (radiofemoral delay) and a systolic murmur heard over the back; femoral pulses here are bounding, not weak.
C. Cardiac tamponade: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds and pulsus paradoxus with a narrow pulse pressure; the opposite of a wide pulse pressure with a murmur.
D. Ventricular septal defect: a harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border; it does not cause a collapsing pulse or a diastolic murmur.
key_concept:
Wide pulse pressure + early diastolic murmur at the left sternal border = aortic regurgitation.
  • Collapsing (water hammer) pulse
  • Pistol-shot femorals, head bobbing, nail bed pulsation
  • Displaced, hyperdynamic apex (LV dilatation)
  • Murmur loudest sitting forward in expiration
  • Severe AR may add an Austin Flint apical rumble
exam_pearl: Bounding femorals point to AR; weak or delayed femorals point to coarctation.

stem: A 66-year-old man presents with a diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge. On examination, the apex beat is displaced outwards. Which condition typically presents with these findings?
highlight_terms_source: diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge
why_right: Of the options, only aortic regurgitation gives a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge (early decrescendo). The outwardly displaced apex fits too: chronic AR volume-overloads the left ventricle, which dilates and pushes the apex beat laterally and downward.
why_wrong_block:
A. Coarctation of the aorta: arm hypertension, radiofemoral delay and a systolic murmur over the back; it does not typically cause a diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge.
C. Mitral regurgitation: can also displace the apex through LV dilatation, but its murmur is pansystolic at the apex radiating to the axilla, not diastolic.
D. Aortic stenosis: an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border; pressure overload gives a heaving but usually non-displaced apex.
key_concept:
Diastolic murmurs: ARMS (left: AR, MS) and PaRTS (right: PR, TS).
  • Early decrescendo diastolic: AR or PR
  • Mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap: MS or TS
  • Volume overload (AR, MR): displaced apex
  • Pressure overload (AS, hypertension): heaving, non-displaced apex
exam_pearl: Decide systolic vs diastolic first; that alone removes MR and AS here.

stem: 56-year-old man has a low-pitched diastolic rumble heard at the apex, a widened pulse pressure and a grade 3/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: low-pitched diastolic rumble heard at the apex
diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border
why_right: The grade 3/6 diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border plus a widened pulse pressure is aortic regurgitation. The low-pitched apical diastolic rumble is the trap: in severe AR the regurgitant jet hits the anterior mitral leaflet and impairs its opening, producing an Austin Flint murmur without any true mitral valve disease.
why_wrong_block:
A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal edge that increases with Valsalva and standing; no diastolic decrescendo murmur and no wide pulse pressure.
B. Pulmonic insufficiency: does give a decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left sternal border, louder on inspiration, but it does not widen the systemic pulse pressure; right in pulmonary hypertension (Graham Steell) or after tetralogy repair.
D. Mitral stenosis: explains an apical rumble, usually with an opening snap and loud S1, but not the decrescendo murmur or the wide pulse pressure.
key_concept:
Apical diastolic rumble + wide pulse pressure + decrescendo diastolic murmur = AR with Austin Flint murmur.
  • Austin Flint: functional mitral inflow obstruction in severe AR, no opening snap
  • True MS: opening snap, loud S1, often rheumatic, atrial fibrillation
  • AR vs PR: wide pulse pressure means AR; louder with inspiration means PR
exam_pearl: Do not jump to mitral stenosis because of an apical rumble when the pulse pressure is wide.

stem: A 28-year-old man who recently joined military service and underwent excessive military training presents to the Emergency Department with lightheadedness on standing and fatigue. Physical examination reveals postural hypotension, otherwise unremarkable. Urine osmolality is elevated > 500 mosmol/L (see lab results). What is the most likely etiology for his acute kidney injury?
why_right: Excessive military training causes volume loss, and postural hypotension confirms hypovolemia. A urine osmolality > 500 means the tubules are intact and concentrating urine maximally, which defines pre-renal azotemia.
why_wrong_block:
B. AIN is intrinsic renal injury; damaged tubules cannot concentrate, so urine osmolality is low (< 300), and it usually follows a drug.
C. Glomerulonephritis is intrinsic renal disease with hematuria, RBC casts, edema and hypertension rather than postural hypotension.
D. ATN can follow prolonged hypovolemia, but tubular damage gives dilute urine (< 300) and FeNa > 2%; a concentrated urine means the tubules still work.
key_concept:
Pre-renal vs intrinsic AKI indices:
  • Urine osmolality: > 500 pre-renal; < 300 intrinsic
  • FeNa: < 1% pre-renal; > 2% ATN
  • Urine Na: low pre-renal; high ATN
  • BUN:Cr: > 20 pre-renal
  • Sediment: bland pre-renal; muddy brown casts ATN
exam_pearl: Concentrated urine (> 500) = tubules working = pre-renal; if exertion also gave dark urine and high CK, think rhabdomyolysis.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 3× in this file (also AS-0004, AS-1417B).

stem: Patient 22 with symptoms of MS (pain on ocular movement and tingling sensation in upper limb) for 4 months, he is now asymptomatic. What is the INITIAL DIAGNOSTIC TEST?
why_right: "Pain on ocular movement" is optic neuritis and "tingling in the upper limb" is a separate sensory lesion, so this young patient has had CNS episodes suggesting multiple sclerosis. The initial diagnostic test is MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium, looking for periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions that show dissemination in space and time. Being asymptomatic now does not matter, because old plaques remain visible on MRI.
why_wrong_block:
A. CSF analysis: oligoclonal bands support the diagnosis and can substitute for dissemination in time, but it is a supportive second-line test after MRI, not the initial one.
C. CT brain: insensitive for demyelinating plaques and cannot image the cord well; right for acute trauma or suspected hemorrhage, not for MS.
key_concept:
Suspected MS: MRI brain and spine first.
  • Typical presentations: optic neuritis, partial myelitis, brainstem syndrome, internuclear ophthalmoplegia
  • MRI: periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord T2 lesions
  • CSF oligoclonal bands: supportive
  • Visual evoked potentials: show subclinical optic nerve involvement
  • Acute relapse: high-dose IV methylprednisolone
exam_pearl: Initial test for suspected MS is MRI; CSF only supports the diagnosis.

stem: Case of lung cancer. They said adenocarcinoma 2 cm in the apical region and no other lesion in any other place. Brain MRI normal. What's the treatment?
highlight_terms_source: no other lesion in any other place
why_right: A 2 cm adenocarcinoma (non-small cell lung cancer) with no other lesion and a normal brain MRI is early-stage, localised disease, and the treatment with curative intent is surgical resection (lobectomy with lymph node sampling). Before surgery the patient still needs complete staging (PET-CT, mediastinal node assessment) and pulmonary function tests to confirm fitness.
why_wrong_block:
B. Chemotherapy: the main treatment for advanced or metastatic disease, or adjuvant therapy after resection when nodes are involved; not the primary treatment for a small localised tumour.
C. Radiotherapy: stereotactic radiotherapy is the alternative for early-stage disease when the patient is medically unfit for surgery or refuses it; this patient has no such barrier.
D. Observation: never appropriate for biopsy-proven cancer; surveillance is for small indeterminate nodules, not a confirmed adenocarcinoma.
key_concept:
NSCLC treatment follows stage.
  • Early localised (stage I to II): surgical resection
  • Early but inoperable: stereotactic body radiotherapy
  • Locally advanced (stage III): chemoradiation with or without surgery
  • Metastatic (stage IV): systemic therapy (chemo, targeted, immunotherapy)
  • Before resection: staging and pulmonary function tests
  • Small cell lung cancer: chemotherapy based; surgery only for rare very early node negative disease
exam_pearl: If the histology were small cell, the answer would usually flip to chemotherapy.

stem: Diabetic with polyuria and polydipsia and family hx of diabetes. HbA1c 7. something. FBG high (I think 9). First-line management?
why_right: A symptomatic patient ("polyuria and polydipsia") with HbA1c 7 point something, a high fasting glucose and a family history has type 2 diabetes. Metformin plus lifestyle change is the first-line drug: it lowers glucose without weight gain or hypoglycaemia, is cheap and has long-term cardiovascular safety data. Other agents are added on top of metformin when targets are not met.
why_wrong_block:
B. Semaglutide or sitagliptin (the recall spelling is unclear): both are add-on agents after metformin; a GLP-1 agonist is chosen early when there is established cardiovascular disease or obesity is a priority, which this stem does not state.
C. Gliclazide or glibenclamide (sulfonylurea): an effective second-line agent but causes hypoglycaemia and weight gain, so it is not first line.
key_concept:
Type 2 diabetes by HbA1c at diagnosis:
  • Above 10% or catabolic symptoms: insulin
  • 7.5 to 10%: metformin with lifestyle
  • Below 7.5%: lifestyle for 3 to 6 months, then metformin if above target
  • Symptomatic patients: start metformin with lifestyle
  • eGFR below 30: do not start metformin
  • ASCVD, heart failure or CKD: add SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist
exam_pearl: Very high HbA1c, weight loss or ketosis shifts the first step from metformin to insulin.

stem: Pt female 20 something. BP: 150/(80 something). Medically free. On examination: flank bruit. Investigation to confirm her diagnosis:
why_right: Hypertension in a young woman (20s) who is "medically free", with an abdominal or flank bruit, points to renal artery stenosis from fibromuscular dysplasia. To confirm the diagnosis you need to image the renal arteries, and the abdominal CT here means CT angiography, which shows the typical "string of beads" narrowing. Catheter renal angiography remains the gold standard and is used when intervention (angioplasty) is planned.
why_wrong_block:
B. Plain abdominal radiograph: shows calcification or stones but cannot see renal artery narrowing; useless for renovascular hypertension.
C. Renal US: plain ultrasound may only show asymmetric kidney size; duplex Doppler ultrasound is a good non-invasive screening test, but it is operator-dependent and less able to confirm FMD than CT angiography.
key_concept:
Secondary hypertension clue: bruit + young age = renal artery stenosis.
  • Young woman: fibromuscular dysplasia, "string of beads" in mid or distal renal artery
  • Older smoker with atherosclerosis: atherosclerotic stenosis at the ostium
  • Screen: duplex Doppler ultrasound
  • Confirm: CT or MR angiography; catheter angiography is gold standard
  • FMD treatment: percutaneous angioplasty without stent
  • ACE inhibitor causing a sharp creatinine rise suggests bilateral stenosis
exam_pearl: Screen with duplex ultrasound, confirm with CT angiography; read "confirm" in the lead-in.

stem: Hepatitis serology: Positive HBsAg, Negative HBsAb, Positive HBcAb IgG, Negative HBcAb IgM, Positive HBeAg. What's management?
key_concept:
Read HBV serology marker by marker.
  • HBsAg+: current infection (acute or chronic)
  • IgM anti-HBc+: acute; IgG anti-HBc+ with HBsAg+: chronic
  • Anti-HBs+ alone: vaccinated; anti-HBs+ with anti-HBc+: recovered
  • HBeAg+: high replication and infectivity; anti-HBe+: lower infectivity
  • Chronic HBV work-up: HBV DNA, ALT, liver fibrosis assessment; treat with tenofovir or entecavir if criteria met
  • Exposed non-immune person or newborn of carrier mother: HBIG + vaccine
exam_pearl: HBIG is prophylaxis for the exposed person (or the baby), never treatment for the person who already carries HBsAg.

stem: A 40 YO male who had "A" relative (didn't determine degree of relative) diagnosed with colon cancer at age of 50 is concerned about colon cancer screening.
key_concept:
Family history changes the start age, and sometimes the interval.
  • Average risk: start at 45 (choose 50 if 45 is not offered), colonoscopy every 10 years
  • First-degree relative with CRC before 60 (or two first-degree relatives): colonoscopy at 40 or 10 years before the youngest diagnosis, every 5 years
  • Second-degree relative only: treat as average risk
  • Other average-risk tools: flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography every 5 years, FOBT yearly
exam_pearl: "Relative" without a degree is the trap: first-degree moves screening to 40; second-degree leaves the patient at average risk.

stem: A 17-year-old man is evaluated in the Emergency Department for polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia and an unintentional weight loss over the past month. He has abdominal pain and drowsiness for the last 21 hours. His medical and family history are unremarkable. He is not on any medications. On physical examination, he looks sick with dry mucous membrane, tachypnea, and tachycardia with clear chest auscultation. Abdominal examination shows diffuse mild tenderness with normal bowel sounds. Intravenous 0.9% saline is initiated. An electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia 120/min. Chest radiograph is normal (see lab results). Blood pressure 95/53 mmHg. Heart rate 119/min. Respiratory rate 20/min. Temperature 37.2 C. Oxygen saturation 95%. BMI 19 kg/m2. Sodium 130 (134-146 mmol/L). Potassium 4.4 (3.5-5.1 mmol/L). Chloride 96 (97-108 mmol/L). Bicarbonate 10 (21-28 mmol/L). Blood urea nitrogen 15 (2.8-8.9 mmol/L). Creatinine 115 (44-115 umol/L). Random glucose 25 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L). ABG: HCO3 10 (22-28 mmol/L), pH 7.10 (7.36-7.45). RBC 5 (4.7-6.1 x10^12/L male; 4.2-5.4 female). Hb 130 (130-170 g/L male; 120-160 female). WBC 14 (4.5-10.5 x10^9/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in the management?
why_right: Glucose 25, pH 7.10 and bicarbonate 10 with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss in a 17-year-old is diabetic ketoacidosis from new-onset type 1 diabetes. Saline has "already been initiated" and potassium is 4.4 (not below 3.3), so the next step is IV insulin to stop ketogenesis and lower glucose, with potassium added to fluids as it falls.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV ceftriaxone: afebrile with a clear chest and normal radiograph; mild leukocytosis is common in DKA. Antibiotics are right only when an infective trigger is found.
C. IV potassium chloride: K 4.4 is normal; potassium is added to the fluids once insulin starts and K falls. Replacing potassium before insulin is needed only when K is below 3.3.
D. IV sodium bicarbonate: reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); pH 7.10 corrects with fluids and insulin.
key_concept:
DKA order: fluids, check K, insulin, then treat the trigger.
  • Diagnosis: hyperglycemia + metabolic acidosis + ketosis
  • Step 1: 0.9% saline resuscitation
  • K below 3.3: replace potassium before insulin
  • K 3.3 or above: start IV insulin infusion (low dose, 0.1 IU/kg/hr)
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Then find the precipitant (missed insulin, infection)
exam_pearl: If the stem had K below 3.3, potassium replacement would come before insulin.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: B (MG).

stem: A patient presents with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). Laboratory results show: Blood glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, Bicarbonate 15 mEq/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
why_right: The labs confirm DKA (glucose 380 mg/dl, pH 7.15, bicarbonate 15). The initial management is IV fluid resuscitation plus IV regular insulin infusion, after checking potassium is not low, because fluids correct the profound dehydration and fixed-rate IV insulin stops ketogenesis and closes the anion gap.
why_wrong_block:
A. IV bicarbonate is reserved for very severe acidosis (pH below 6.9); at pH 7.15 it adds no benefit and risks hypokalemia and paradoxical CNS acidosis.
B. Subcutaneous insulin is used once DKA has resolved (overlapping with the infusion before stopping it); absorption is unreliable in a dehydrated acidotic patient, so it is not the initial treatment here.
key_concept:
DKA ladder: fluids, potassium, insulin, find the trigger.
  • Fluids first: 0.9% saline bolus, then 0.45% saline
  • Check K: if below 3.3, replace before insulin
  • Regular insulin IV infusion 0.1 U/kg/hr
  • Add dextrose when glucose falls, continue insulin until acidosis resolves
  • Bicarbonate only if pH below 6.9
  • Switch to SC basal insulin with overlap once resolved
exam_pearl: If the options separate fluids from insulin, fluids alone come first; if potassium is low, potassium comes before insulin.

Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0693).
Compiler note: Related variant listed under 2536 (Q: block).

stem: A 50-year-old man is complaining of pain affecting the wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints, and right knee joint for the last 4 months. His examination revealed active arthritis at both wrists and second and third proximal interphalangeal joints (see lab results). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
highlight_terms_source: wrist joints bilaterally, second and third proximal interphalangeal joints
why_right: Symmetric arthritis of both wrists and 2nd/3rd PIPs for 4 months with active arthritis on exam is new rheumatoid arthritis. This recall's key combines DMARD maintenance (methotrexate as the anchor, with hydroxychloroquine) and short-term prednisone as a bridge, because steroids control synovitis within days while DMARDs take weeks to months to work. The steroid is then tapered once the DMARDs take effect.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate: the correct anchor DMARD, but alone it gives no rapid control of active synovitis while it takes effect; in this recall the bridge is the missing piece.
B. Methotrexate and sulfasalazine: an acceptable DMARD combination, but it still lacks the steroid bridge for active arthritis.
C. Methotrexate and hydroxychloroquine: good maintenance DMARDs, but no bridging glucocorticoid for the currently active joints.
key_concept:
New active RA = DMARD (methotrexate based) for maintenance + short-term prednisone as a bridge.
  • Methotrexate is the cornerstone; hydroxychloroquine alone is not enough
  • Steroids act in days, DMARDs in weeks to months
  • Taper steroids once controlled; do not continue long term
  • Refractory or erosive disease: add a TNF inhibitor
  • Anti-CCP confirms RA; RA spares DIP joints
exam_pearl: When the stem says 'active arthritis' at diagnosis, choose the option that includes the steroid bridge.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: D (GB). Lab results referenced but not shown.

stem: Child fell from tree, vomiting, head swelling, he became drowsy. What is the MOST APPROPRIATE management?
why_right: A child who fell from a tree, is vomiting and has "become drowsy" has a deteriorating level of consciousness after head injury. Trauma care follows ABC, so securing the airway (intubation) to protect against aspiration and hypoxia comes before any definitive neurosurgical step. The hematoma has not even been confirmed on CT yet.
why_wrong_block: A. Hematoma evacuation: needs a CT showing a surgical lesion (e.g. epidural hematoma with midline shift) and a secured airway; it becomes the answer when the stem already gives that CT and the airway is not the problem.
key_concept:
Head injury with falling consciousness: Airway first, then CT, then surgery.
  • Intubate: GCS 8 or less, unconscious, SpO2 below 88%, or aspiration risk (vomiting with drowsiness)
  • Then non-contrast CT head
  • Epidural hematoma: lens-shaped, middle meningeal artery, lucid interval
  • Surgical hematoma with mass effect: craniotomy and evacuation
exam_pearl: When the stem gives no CT and only symptoms of deterioration, the answer is the airway; when it gives CT with midline shift and a stable child, the answer is evacuation.

stem: 12/16 years old girl fall 2 meters while playing, The loss of consciousness then vomited many times and then become sleepy, in examination there is head hematoma and left limb weakness and sign of lateralization, CT brain show extra dural hematoma with midline shift. ( no GCS in the Qs) What is the best next management?
OptD: repeat the CT scan after 12 hours.
highlight_terms_source: left limb weakness and sign of lateralization
extra dural hematoma with midline shift
why_right: Fall from 2 meters, loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, sleepiness, "left limb weakness" and lateralizing signs with CT showing an "extradural hematoma with midline shift" means a surgical lesion with mass effect. The definitive and time-critical treatment is urgent craniotomy and hematoma evacuation; midline shift over 5 mm is an accepted indication.
why_wrong_block:
B. Intubate and secure the airway: the first step when GCS is 8 or less or the airway is at risk, and it may be done on the way to theatre, but no GCS is given and the question has already reached the CT stage; the decision being tested is surgery.
C. Admit and observe: right for a small epidural hematoma without midline shift or neurological deficit in an alert patient; focal weakness and shift rule it out.
D. Repeat CT after 12 hours: right for a minor stable lesion being monitored; waiting with lateralizing signs and shift risks herniation and death.
key_concept:
Epidural hematoma: arterial bleed that needs evacuation once it causes mass effect.
  • Source: middle meningeal artery (temporal fracture)
  • CT: biconvex, lens-shaped
  • Clinical: lucid interval, ipsilateral blown pupil, contralateral weakness
  • Midline shift over 5 mm or focal deficit: craniotomy and evacuation
  • Small, no shift, alert: observe with repeat CT
exam_pearl: CT already showing shift plus lateralizing signs moves the answer from airway or observation to evacuation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Short version: child fell from 2 meters, vomiting multiple times and sleepy, left side weakness, CT shows extradural hemorrhage; options hematoma evacuation (highlighted) vs intubate and secure the airway. Related: Hematoma with 6mm midline shift -> Craniotomy. Midline shift > 5mm -> Craniotomy.

stem: 28-year-old patient presented to the clinic complaining of perianal discharge. He reported history of on-off abdominal pain. He reported family history of Crohn's disease. On examination, three fistula openings at 3, 7 and 9 o'clock. What is the most appropriate next step?
why_right: A 28-year-old with "three fistula openings", recurrent abdominal pain and a family history of Crohn's has multiple, complex perianal fistulae that point to undiagnosed Crohn's disease. This recall's key is colonoscopy (with ileoscopy and biopsies) to confirm the underlying disease, because fistula management is very different in Crohn's (medical therapy, setons, avoiding fistulotomy).
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI: the gold-standard imaging to map fistula tracts and find abscesses; it is the answer when Crohn's is already known and the question asks for fistula anatomy or a suspected abscess.
C. Fistulogram: an older, less accurate way to outline a tract, largely replaced by MRI and endoanal ultrasound.
D. US: endoanal ultrasound can assess simple tracts and sphincters, but transabdominal US does not diagnose Crohn's or map complex perianal disease.
key_concept:
Multiple or recurrent perianal fistulae: think Crohn's.
  • Suspected Crohn's not yet diagnosed: colonoscopy with ileoscopy and biopsy
  • Fistula anatomy or abscess: MRI pelvis
  • Abscess: drain before escalating immunosuppression
  • Fistulizing Crohn's: anti-TNF (infliximab), setons
  • Simple low non-Crohn's fistula: fistulotomy
exam_pearl: Known Crohn's with perianal sepsis: MRI pelvis; suspected but undiagnosed Crohn's: colonoscopy.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-2100B).

stem: concerning and warrants further evaluation for possible malignancy. Which of the following types of nipple discharge is most concerning?
OptD: Spontaneous unilateral, from a single duct, and clear
why_right: Pathological nipple discharge is "spontaneous", "unilateral" and from a "single duct", and is usually serous (clear) or bloody. These three features suggest a localized ductal lesion (intraductal papilloma or carcinoma) and need imaging and evaluation whatever the colour. The other options each have a feature that makes them physiological or benign.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spontaneous and bilateral red: blood is worrying, but bilateral, multi-duct discharge suggests a systemic or diffuse benign process; unilateral single-duct bloody discharge would be the concerning version (classically intraductal papilloma).
B. Spontaneous bilateral milky: galactorrhea from prolactin excess, drugs, pregnancy or lactation; it needs a prolactin and drug review, not a malignancy work-up.
C. Induced unilateral green: discharge produced by squeezing, especially green or dark, is typical of duct ectasia or fibrocystic change and is benign.
key_concept:
Nipple discharge red flags: spontaneous, unilateral, single duct, bloody or serous.
  • Physiological: bilateral, multi-duct, expressed only, milky or green
  • Bloody single duct: intraductal papilloma most common cause
  • Green/dark with inverted nipple: duct ectasia
  • Milky bilateral: galactorrhea (check prolactin, drugs, pregnancy)
  • Pathological pattern: imaging (US with or without mammogram), then biopsy or duct excision
exam_pearl: Colour alone does not make discharge malignant; spontaneity, laterality and single-duct origin do.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Stem is truncated in the source (begins mid-sentence).

stem: child was riding a bicycle, and then he sustained a handlebar injury, he presented to the ER with abdominal pain and tenderness And Nausea & Vomiting FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive. What’s Most Likely Injured Abdominal Organ?
highlight_terms_source: FAST Was Done And It Was Inconclusive
why_right: A "handlebar injury" is a focused blow to the epigastrium that crushes the pancreas (and duodenum) against the vertebral column, classically in children. The pancreas is retroperitoneal, so FAST is often "inconclusive" because early free intraperitoneal fluid may be absent; CT abdomen with contrast is the test when this is suspected.
why_wrong_block:
A. Spleen: the most commonly injured solid organ in blunt abdominal trauma overall, with left upper quadrant pain and usually free fluid on FAST; the handlebar mechanism points elsewhere.
B. Liver: commonly injured in right upper quadrant blows and usually produces hemoperitoneum visible on FAST.
D. Urinary bladder: injured with pelvic fractures or a blow to a full bladder, presenting with hematuria or inability to void, not an epigastric handlebar impact.
key_concept:
Mechanism predicts organ in blunt trauma.
  • Handlebar (epigastric) blow: pancreas and duodenum
  • Retroperitoneal injury: FAST may be negative or inconclusive
  • Suspected pancreatic or duodenal injury, stable: CT abdomen with contrast
  • Lap belt: small bowel, mesentery, lumbar (Chance) fracture
  • Overall most common solid organ: spleen
exam_pearl: "Most commonly injured organ" in blunt trauma is spleen, but a handlebar mechanism with negative FAST is pancreas.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer: C. Pancreas ✅ (also highlighted; 'Soft tissue' written beside C). Handlebar injury (direct epigastric blow) causes pancreatic injury, especially in children. FAST is often inconclusive because pancreatic injuries are retroperitoneal and may not produce significant free intraperitoneal fluid early. UpToDate, ATLS (may not be detected on FAST; CT abdomen with contrast if suspected), Nelson.

stem: A diabetic patient presents with a NON-HEALING foot ulcer. The patient complains of numbness. On exam, The ulcer shows central erythema. (no mention of "with signs of healing", no mention of pulse). He's unable to perceive touch and sensation. What is the most critical test to perform to reach the diagnosis?
why_right: The stem already shows neuropathy ("numbness", "unable to perceive touch"), so the open question for a "NON-HEALING" diabetic ulcer with no pulse findings given is whether the limb has enough blood supply. Peripheral arterial disease is the main reason a diabetic ulcer fails to heal, and the ABI is the critical bedside test for it; it decides referral for revascularization and whether the wound can heal.
why_wrong_block:
B. Monofilament test: screens for loss of protective sensation; it is the answer for routine diabetic foot screening, but here the sensory loss is already evident and does not explain failure to heal.
C. Assessment of pressure points: important for offloading and preventing ulcers, but it does not diagnose the cause of a non-healing ulcer.
key_concept:
Non-healing diabetic foot ulcer: check perfusion first.
  • First step: palpate pulses, then ABI
  • ABI 0.9 to 1.4: normal; below 0.9: PAD; below 0.5: severe
  • ABI above 1.4: calcified vessels (common in diabetes), use toe pressures or Doppler
  • Absent pulse: arterial Doppler; intact pulse with dark skin: venous duplex
  • Monofilament: annual neuropathy screening
exam_pearl: In diabetics a falsely high ABI from calcified arteries can hide PAD; that is when toe pressures or Doppler are used.

stem: A 12-year-old presents with left sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender left testis with redness and edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A 12-year-old with lower abdominal pain and a slightly elevated, tender testis has testicular torsion: the twisted cord pulls the testis upward, and adolescent torsion commonly refers pain to the lower abdomen. Redness and edema of the scrotum come from venous congestion. The alternate recall adds an absent cremasteric reflex and no transillumination, which point the same way.
why_wrong_block:
B. Epididymo-orchitis has a gradual onset with fever or urinary symptoms, a preserved cremasteric reflex and pain relieved by elevation; the testis is not high riding. Think of it in a sexually active young man, or in a child with a UTI or urinary tract anomaly.
C. An incarcerated inguinal hernia is a tender, irreducible lump that extends from the scrotum up into the groin, typically in an infant; here the finding is an elevated tender testis, not a groin mass.
D. Torsion of a testicular appendage gives tenderness localized to the upper pole (blue dot sign) with a normally positioned, vertical testis; the whole testis being elevated and tender points to true torsion.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: decide by testis position, reflex and site of tenderness.
  • Torsion: sudden, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • Appendage torsion: upper pole tenderness, blue dot, vertical testis
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever, dysuria, reflex present
  • Incarcerated hernia: irreducible tender lump into the groin
  • Torsion: urgent exploration, imaging must not delay surgery
exam_pearl: Vertical testis with focal upper pole tenderness flips the answer to appendage torsion; an elevated whole testis keeps it at torsion.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Alternate recall (Q:): sudden hemiscrotal pain with swelling and tenderness, cremasteric reflex absent, no transillumination (didn't mention 'high riding'): A testicular torsion (highlighted), B epididymo-orchitis, C hydrocele.

stem: Elderly women with previous laparotomy for sigmoidectomy after complicated diverticulitis, with incisional hernia symptomatic painful What is the best next step?
why_right: An incisional hernia after a previous laparotomy that is symptomatic and painful needs repair, and incisional hernias are repaired with mesh because suture repair alone has a high recurrence rate. A laparoscopic approach with mesh reinforcement gives a lower wound infection rate and faster recovery, which suits an elderly patient with a scarred abdomen.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is only for a small asymptomatic hernia in a patient unfit or unwilling for surgery; this hernia is painful, so it should be repaired.
B. Open repair without mesh (primary suture) has an unacceptably high recurrence for incisional hernias; tissue repair is reserved for very small defects or a contaminated field where mesh is avoided.
C. Laparoscopic repair is the right approach, but without mesh it is incomplete: the laparoscopic incisional repair is by definition a mesh repair, so the option that names the mesh is the best answer.
key_concept:
Symptomatic hernia = repair; incisional hernia = mesh.
  • Laparoscopic mesh indications: bilateral, recurrent, need for fast recovery, incisional/ventral
  • Primary unilateral inguinal hernia in a fit patient: open mesh repair
  • Suture repair alone: high recurrence for incisional hernias
  • Strangulated or obstructed hernia: emergency surgery
exam_pearl: When one option says repair and another says the same repair with mesh, the mesh option wins for an incisional hernia.

stem: Old female + Weight loss & Stool +ve for occult blood + Constipation
why_right: An older woman with weight loss, change in bowel habit (constipation) and a positive fecal occult blood test has colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. A positive occult blood test always needs a full colonoscopy, which views the entire colon, allows biopsy and detects synchronous lesions.
why_wrong_block: A. Sigmoidoscopy only examines the rectum and sigmoid, so a right sided (proximal) tumor, which often presents with occult bleeding and anemia, would be missed. Even when sigmoidoscopy finds a distal cancer, a full colonoscopy is still required to look for synchronous tumors.
key_concept:
Positive FOBT or red flags (age, weight loss, bowel habit change, iron deficiency anemia) = colonoscopy.
  • Colonoscopy: whole colon, biopsy, synchronous lesions
  • Cancer found on sigmoidoscopy: next step colonoscopy, then CT chest/abdomen/pelvis for staging
  • Iron deficiency anemia in an older adult: upper and lower GI endoscopy
  • Multiple liver lesions with constitutional symptoms: colonoscopy to find the primary
exam_pearl: Occult blood plus weight loss is never followed up with a limited scope; the answer is the full colonoscopy.
